**A. Avoid benzodiazepines categorically.** Worsened confusion matters in routine delirium care. Severe refractory distress near death is a distinct indication for sedation.
**B. Prefer long-acting diazepam.** Accumulation and prolonged sedation make it harder to adjust the balance between comfort and alertness.
**C. Insist on the oral route.** Route depends on swallowing and clinical need. Parenteral routes are possible.
**D. Short-acting midazolam with titration.** Short action and adjustment to symptom relief match the therapeutic aim. Discuss the effect on communication and breathing.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 890
chapterTitle: PALLIATIVE CARE AND SPECIAL MANAGEMENT ISSUES

q: בת 73, מגיעה למיון עם קוצר נשימה, החמרה במצבה בחודש האחרון, ירידה תפקודית, וסחרחורת במאמץ מינימאלי מזה כשבוע. אשפוזים חוזרים בחצי שנה האחרונה עקב החמרת אי. ספיקת לב רקע: • מחלת לב איסכמית – ניתוח מעקפים לפני כ- 10 שנים, צנתור אחרון במהלך אשפוזה הקודם עם התערבות למעקפים ופתיחתם • מחלת כלי דם היקפיים • סוכרת מטופלת במשתנים במינונים מקסימאליים, SACUBITRIL/VALSARTAN (ENTRESTO) במינון מקסימאלי וב- SGLT2. בבדיקה - לחץ דם 125/80, דופק 105, נשימות 24. מעבדה - BUN 23, קריאטינין 1.5 בהחמרה מבסיס. אק"ג - סינוס טכיקרדיה ללא הפרעת הולכה. אקוקרדיוגרפיה - חדר שמאל מורחב עם מקטע פליטה 20%, ואי ספיקה מיטראלית קלה. מה מהבאים יכול לשפר את איכות חייה ויאריך אותם ?
o: השתלת קוצב – Cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT)
מכשיר תומך בחדר שמאל - Left ventricular assisted device (LVAD)
תיקון מסתם מיטראלי – Mitral Clip
אין מה שיכול לשפר את מצבה, מומלץ להעבירה לטיפול פליאטיבי בלבד.
explanation:
An LVAD provides mechanical circulatory support for selected patients with advanced systolic heart failure. **Evaluate for LVAD candidacy** given EF 20%, recurrent admissions and symptoms despite intensive treatment.

**A. CRT.** Benefit generally requires qualifying electrical dyssynchrony. No conduction disturbance is described.
**B. LVAD.** It may improve survival and function, but renal disease, vascular disease, frailty and goals affect candidacy.
**C. MitraClip.** Mild mitral regurgitation is insufficient to explain the severe failure or justify repair.
**D. Palliative care alone.** Palliative support is valuable and can accompany evaluation for advanced treatment.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1184, 1189.

q: בן 83 סובל מהידרדרות תפקודית וקוגניטיבית בשנה האחרונה. הוא הולך לאט מאוד, סובל מנפילות חוזרות, סובל מפחד מפני נפילות, ירד במשקל 7 ק"ג בשנה האחרונה, מרגיש עייפות כל הזמן, וגם עולה חשד למחלת אלצהיימר בחומרה בינונית. לפי הקריטריונים של FRIED כיצד ניתן להגדיר את החולה?
o: PREFRAIL
FRAIL
VERY FRAIL
COGNITIVE FRAIL
explanation:
The **Fried frailty phenotype** assesses unintentional weight loss, weak grip, exhaustion, slowness, and low activity. At least three features define frailty; exhaustion, slowing, and weight loss in the stem point to that category (pp. 619–620).

**A. Prefrail.** Wrong, prefrailty precedes accumulation of three criteria; the described features already point toward frailty (pp. 619–620).
**B. Frail.** Correct, this category applies when at least three features are present and is the official classification for this presentation (pp. 619–620).
**C. Very frail.** Wrong, this model does not define a separate category with that name from these findings; a severity term from another model should not replace its classification (pp. 619–620).
**D. Cognitive frail.** Wrong, Fried's physical model has no specific cognitive dimension; suspected Alzheimer disease does not change the requested classification within that model (pp. 619–620).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 619–620, Table 42-2.

q: בת 84 מטופלת במחלקה שיקומית לאחר שבר בצוואר הירך. לאחר חודש של שיקום היא. הולכת עם הליכון בהשגחה בלבד בתחום החדר ומתוכננת להשתחרר למחלקה סיעודית. מה תפקיד הריפוי בעיסוק בשיקום שלה?
o: שליחת צוות לביקור לבדיקת התאמת המסגרת לתפקודה
הערכה קוגניטיבית בשאלה של התאמתה למחלקה לתשושי נפש
שיפור ADL – אכילה, הלבשת פלג גוף עליון, טיפוח
במצב זה אין תועלת בריפוי בעיסוק
explanation:
Occupational therapy helps a patient recover or adapt everyday self-care tasks. Moving to a nursing facility changes the setting where she will use those skills, while the ability to eat, dress and groom herself still matters.

**Train eating, upper-body dressing and grooming. Gains in these activities preserve autonomy and reduce the amount of help she will need each day.**

**A. Visit to assess the facility.** Environmental assessment can be valuable when specific barriers need to be addressed. It does not replace direct training of the patient’s self-care skills.
**B. Cognitive assessment for a dementia unit.** Assess cognition when it affects performance or placement. No new cognitive or behavioral problem here makes classification the immediate therapy goal.
**C. Improve eating, dressing and grooming.** These are concrete activities the therapist can observe, adapt and practice with her before transfer.
**D. No role for occupational therapy.** A continuing need for nursing care can coexist with meaningful gains in selected daily activities.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 823, Table 55-4.
referenceNote: Printed IMA citation retained; checked explanation source: Hazzard 8e · p. 823.

q: מה מהבאים מהווה גורם לאוסטיאופורוזיס שניוני?
o: היפרתירואידיזם
מין – אישה
קורס של 5 ימים של PREDNISONE 30 mg
סוכרת שאינה תלויה באינסולין
explanation:
Secondary osteoporosis is skeletal fragility related to a disease or medication beyond ordinary age-associated loss. **Hyperthyroidism is a classic secondary cause of low bone density.** Excess thyroid hormone accelerates remodeling and promotes net bone loss.

**A. Hyperthyroidism.** Investigate thyroid excess as a reversible contributor in someone with osteoporosis.
**B. Female sex.** It is a population risk factor, not itself a secondary disorder.
**C. Prednisone 30 mg for five days.** Sustained systemic glucocorticoid exposure is the classic cause. This isolated short course is a different exposure.
**D. Type 2 diabetes.** It can impair bone quality and increase fractures despite normal or higher measured BMD. A combined list of contributors to osteoporosis or fractures includes type 2 diabetes because fracture risk can rise without a fall in bone density.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 768–769, Table 51-3. Bone Health and Osteoporosis Foundation Clinician's Guide, 2022, Table 1, doi:10.1007/s00198-021-05900-y.

q: בן 73, עם ציון מינימנטל של 23, איזה מהבאים מחשיד לדמנציה אחרת שאיננה אלצהיימר ?
o: ירידה של 3 נקודות במינימנטל בשנה
המטופל לא מסוגל לכתוב הודעות בטלפון הנייד בשנה האחרונה
הפרעות בשנת ה- REM
קושי בשליפת מילים
explanation:
IMA key (2025-Jun Q96) — **REM sleep disturbances**.

The revised DLB description lists “recurrent visual hallucinations, RBD, and spontaneous features of parkinsonism”. A history of REM dream enactment therefore shifts the differential toward Lewy body disease in a patient with cognitive decline.

**A. A decline of 3 MMSE points per year.** A decline in MMSE over a year can occur with Alzheimer disease and is not distinctive.
**B. Inability to write mobile-phone messages over the past year.** Loss of a complex daily task occurs in many dementias and provides no specific alternative diagnosis.
**C. REM sleep disturbances.** REM sleep behavior disorder is a recognized Lewy body clue. It does not exclude coexisting Alzheimer pathology.
**D. Word-finding difficulty.** Word retrieval difficulty can occur in Alzheimer disease and is less discriminating.

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 900, 981, 984.

q: מה מהבאים לא מוכר כסיבוך של האכלת צינור?
o: עצירות
תמותה
דלקת ריאות
ירידה במשקל
explanation:
Enteral feeding supplies nutrition through a tube but can cause gastrointestinal or respiratory complications. It also does not guarantee weight maintenance or survival in a frail patient.

**None of these outcomes can be reliably excluded as a complication.** Constipation is a recognized gastrointestinal problem, and weight loss, aspiration pneumonia and death have been reported among tube-fed patients with pressure injuries.

**A. Constipation.** Enteral nutrition can be accompanied by constipation. Review hydration, fiber intake, medications and bowel function.
**B. Death.** Severe complications of tube feeding can contribute to death. A death in a tube-fed patient requires clinical attribution because underlying illness also influences survival.
**C. Pneumonia.** Aspiration of refluxed feed or secretions can cause pneumonia despite tube access.
**D. Weight loss.** A feeding tube cannot guarantee delivery or absorption of prescribed calories. Weight loss is specifically reported in this clinical population.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 692. ESPEN guideline on home enteral nutrition, monitoring and complications, 2020.
Key note: All four responses received credit. Hazzard lists weight loss, aspiration pneumonia and death, and ESPEN also recognizes constipation. Each can occur with tube feeding.
keySource: IMA 2025-Jun Subspecialty official answer key after appeals, Q97
label: All answers accepted after appeal

q: מה לא גורם הפיך לאי שליטה על סוגר השתן?
o: מחלת עורקים פריפרית (PVD)
וגיניטיס אטרופית (Vaginitis Atrophic)
היפרקלצמיה
אי ספיקת לב עם בצקת פריפרית
explanation:
Official answer: א

**Peripheral vascular disease** is not listed among the reversible causes of urinary incontinence in Table 47-3. There is no need to invent irreversible structural damage to explain the choice (p. 702).

**A. Peripheral arterial disease (PVD).** Correct, this is the option absent from the reversible-cause table. The choice does not require attributing irreversible structural damage to the disease (p. 702).
**B. Atrophic vaginitis.** Wrong, it is included, and topical estrogen may help; therefore it is not the exception (p. 702).
**C. Hypercalcemia.** Wrong, it can cause polyuria and precipitate leakage, and is a metabolic cause to investigate and treat (p. 702).
**D. Heart failure with peripheral edema.** Wrong, volume expansion can increase nighttime urine production and leakage; the table includes treating this cause in reversible-factor assessment (p. 702).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 702.

q: איזה מהבאים לא מעלה סיכון ל- Deep Vein Thrombosis?
o: טיפול ב- TAMOXIFEN
תסמונת נפרוטית
סרטן לבלב
טיפול תרופתי ב- ESCITALOPRAM ( CIPRALEX)
explanation:
Deep venous thrombosis risk rises in acquired prothrombotic states and with certain medications. **Escitalopram is the exception among these established risk factors**.

**A. Tamoxifen.** This selective estrogen receptor modulator increases venous thromboembolism risk.
**B. Nephrotic syndrome.** Loss of anticoagulant proteins and other coagulation changes promote thrombosis.
**C. Pancreatic cancer.** It is a particularly thrombogenic malignancy.
**D. Escitalopram.** It lacks the characteristic prothrombotic associations of the other three exposures.

CIPROFLOXACIN (CIPRO)
BUPROPION (WELLBUTRIN)
PREGABALIN (LYRICA)
explanation:
Drugs that lower the seizure threshold can provoke breakthrough seizures despite antiseizure treatment. For this man taking levetiracetam, **pregabalin** treats neuropathic pain and is also used as an adjunct for focal seizures.

**B. Ciprofloxacin.** This fluoroquinolone can cause central nervous system excitation and seizures. Impaired renal clearance can increase exposure.

**D. Pregabalin.** It binds the alpha-2-delta subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels and reduces excitatory neurotransmitter release. Adjust for kidney function and watch for dizziness during hip-fracture recovery.

q: An older inpatient has an acute, fluctuating change in mental status. Which additional findings satisfy the CAM algorithm for delirium?
o: Inattention with disorganized thinking or altered consciousness
Disorganized thinking with preserved attention and normal consciousness
Altered consciousness with preserved attention and organized thinking
Inattention with organized thinking and normal consciousness
explanation:
CAM requires an acute or fluctuating change and inattention. The remaining requirement can be met by disorganized thought or a change in arousal.
**With the acute change already present, identify inattention plus either disorganized thinking or altered consciousness.**

**A. Inattention with disorganized thinking or altered consciousness.** This combination completes all required parts of CAM.
**B. Disorganized thinking with preserved attention and normal consciousness.** Disorganized thought cannot substitute for the essential attentional disturbance.
**C. Altered consciousness with preserved attention and organized thinking.** Altered arousal also cannot substitute for impaired attention.
**D. Inattention with organized thinking and normal consciousness.** Inattention alone does not complete the algorithm when thought organization and consciousness are both normal.

q: An older inpatient develops delirium after several psychoactive medications are added. Which interpretation best explains why these drugs need review?
o: Medication effects and interactions represent a potentially remediable precipitant of delirium.
Medication effects and interactions usually leave a persistent, nonremediable cause of delirium.
Increasing the number of prescribed drugs tends to reduce delirium through offsetting effects.
Drug interactions explain delirium better because the drugs themselves lack direct effects.
explanation:
Centrally acting medicines can directly alter attention, and multiple drugs create opportunities for drug–drug and drug–disease interactions. Medication exposure is often modifiable.
**Reconcile the new psychoactive drugs and assess their individual and combined effects.**

**A. Medication effects and interactions represent a potentially remediable precipitant of delirium.** Removing or reducing unnecessary exposure can address a remediable precipitant.
**B. Medication effects and interactions usually leave a persistent, nonremediable cause of delirium.** Drug effects are often among the more readily corrected contributors to delirium.
**C. Increasing the number of prescribed drugs tends to reduce delirium through offsetting effects.** Additional drugs increase exposure and interaction risk. They do not reliably offset one another.
**D. Drug interactions explain delirium better because the drugs themselves lack direct effects.** Direct effects and interactions both matter, even when a single drug has been added.

q: What acute-onset timeframe distinguishes delirium from dementia's insidious course?
o: Up to a year
Hours to days
Weeks to months
A month or more
explanation:
When comparing delirium with dementia, establish the interval over which attention and cognition first changed. Duration of residual symptoms is a separate question.
**Delirium typically begins over hours to days.**

**A. Up to a year.** Cognitive effects can persist for many months, but that describes follow-up rather than usual onset.
**B. Hours to days.** A change developing within hours or a few days strongly favors an acute syndrome.
**C. Weeks to months.** An insidious change over weeks or months favors dementia in the differential table.
**D. A month or more.** Symptoms may persist a month after illness. That is not the typical interval over which delirium starts.

A total score of 0
A total score of 2
A score of 4 or more

The 4AT is a four-item bedside screen for possible delirium. Its total ranges from zero to twelve and must be interpreted with the clinical history.
**A total of four or more suggests possible delirium and prompts clinical assessment.**

**A. A total score of 1.** One is below the delirium screening threshold.
**B. A total score of 0.** Zero does not meet the positive threshold. A single test cannot exclude intermittent symptoms.
**C. A total score of 2.** Two is likewise below the delirium threshold and can reflect cognitive impairment.

o: Fever with clinical suspicion of meningitis
Concern for a subclinical seizure disorder
New focal neurologic findings on examination
A recent change in psychoactive medication
explanation:
Investigations for delirium should follow the bedside findings. Imaging looks for structural disease such as a stroke or subdural collection.
**A new focal neurologic deficit specifically supports brain imaging.**

**A. Fever with clinical suspicion of meningitis.** Suspected meningitis directs assessment toward cerebrospinal fluid when safe.
**B. Concern for a subclinical seizure disorder.** Concern about nonconvulsive seizures directs assessment toward EEG.
**C. New focal neurologic findings on examination.** A new focal sign suggests a structural intracranial process warranting CT or MRI.

o: Melatonin receptor agonists
Antipsychotics
Benzodiazepines
Alpha-2 agonists
explanation:
Sedatives may worsen ordinary delirium, but withdrawal and seizures have a different treatment mechanism. Benzodiazepines can control withdrawal-related excitation and seizure activity.
**Benzodiazepines are the treatment of choice when seizures or alcohol or medication withdrawal cause the delirium.**

**A. Melatonin receptor agonists.** Trials of melatonin agents in delirium have mixed results and they do not treat withdrawal seizures.
**B. Antipsychotics.** Antipsychotics may control selected dangerous behaviors but do not treat a withdrawal syndrome.
**C. Benzodiazepines.** Here a benzodiazepine treats the cause, which explains the exception to routine avoidance.
**D. Alpha-2 agonists.** Alpha-2 agonists have selected ICU roles and do not replace treatment of withdrawal or seizures.

q: What is the single most important, validated risk factor for Alzheimer disease?
o: Low educational attainment
Traumatic brain injury
Advancing chronological age
Habitual physical inactivity
explanation:
A risk factor can be strongly predictive without being modifiable. Both the incidence and the proportion of people living with Alzheimer disease rise sharply across successive older age groups.

**Advancing chronological age** has the strongest established association with Alzheimer risk across older adults.

**A. Less education.** Limited schooling is associated with higher risk, possibly through differences in cognitive reserve, but age has the stronger overall association.
**B. Traumatic brain injury.** A history of head injury can raise susceptibility, especially with severe or repeated injury. It is not the dominant predictor across older adults.
**C. Advancing age.** The steep age gradient applies across a broad range of backgrounds and exposures.
**D. Physical inactivity.** Inactivity is a modifiable midlife risk, useful for prevention counseling, but less important than age as an overall predictor.

q: Hazzard links midlife physical inactivity and obesity to later Alzheimer disease. Which interpretation of their relationship is supported?
o: They are interrelated factors that each independently increase later AD risk
Inactivity affects AD risk through obesity without an independent association
Obesity affects AD risk through inactivity without an independent association
Their association is confined to vascular dementia rather than later AD
explanation:
Physical inactivity and obesity frequently coexist in midlife. An independent association means that the relationship of one exposure with later Alzheimer disease is not fully explained by the other.

**Each is independently associated with later Alzheimer risk, even though the two are interrelated.** Ask about both activity and weight when reviewing midlife exposures.

**A. Interrelated but independent.** Their co-occurrence leaves room for each to contribute separate information about later risk.
**B. Inactivity solely through obesity.** Lower activity can be associated with risk even after accounting for obesity.
**C. Obesity solely through inactivity.** Obesity likewise has an association beyond physical inactivity.
**D. Vascular dementia alone.** Midlife vascular and metabolic factors are associated with later Alzheimer disease as well as cerebrovascular disease.

q: Roughly what fraction of AD cases worldwide might be attributable to potentially modifiable risk factors?
o: About 78%
More than 95%
About one-third
About 1-5%
explanation:
A population-attributable fraction estimates how much disease in a population might be associated with particular exposures. It cannot predict how much one person's risk will fall after a lifestyle change.

**About one-third of Alzheimer cases worldwide** were estimated to be potentially attributable to modifiable risk factors.

**A. About 78%.** This percentage describes the share of familial Alzheimer mutations attributed to PSEN1, a different denominator.
**B. More than 95%.** This is the approximate share of Alzheimer cases with late onset. It does not measure modifiable exposures.
**C. About one-third.** This estimate concerns potentially modifiable factors across the worldwide population with Alzheimer disease.
**D. About 1% to 5%.** This describes the much smaller familial share of all Alzheimer cases.

q: Which gene accounts for the majority of familial (early-onset) AD mutations?
o: PSEN1
APP
PSEN2
MAPT
explanation:
Three principal autosomal dominant familial Alzheimer genes affect amyloid precursor protein or its processing. The frequency question concerns identified familial mutations, a small subset of all Alzheimer disease.

**PSEN1 accounts for the largest share, approximately 78%.** Its protein, presenilin-1, participates in the enzyme complex that cleaves amyloid precursor protein.

**A. PSEN1.** Pathogenic variants are the commonest of the three familial mutation groups.
**B. APP.** APP mutations account for a smaller share, about 18%, despite the central role of its protein in amyloid biology.
**C. PSEN2.** Presenilin-2 mutations account for a still smaller share, about 4%.
**D. MAPT.** Pathogenic variants in the tau gene are associated with familial frontotemporal dementia rather than this group of Alzheimer mutations.

q: Hazzard reports discordance between a clinical Alzheimer dementia diagnosis and autopsy findings. In its discussion of the 2018 research framework, what is the implication for trials of disease-modifying treatment?
o: Select participants by symptoms alone because the clinical syndrome establishes the pathology
Select participants without biological characterization because pathology does not affect efficacy assessment
Select participants with biological confirmation to evaluate treatment in the intended disease
Select participants with non-AD cognitive syndromes because these establish the same biological diagnosis
explanation:
An Alzheimer-like cognitive syndrome can arise without the amyloid plaques and tau tangles a disease-modifying drug is intended to target. Autopsy studies found this mismatch in roughly 10% to 30% of people diagnosed clinically with Alzheimer dementia.

**Enroll participants with biological confirmation of the target disease.** Otherwise, including people who lack the target can dilute an apparent treatment effect or obscure its interpretation.

**A. Symptoms alone.** Typical memory loss identifies a clinical phenotype, but it cannot guarantee the underlying pathology.
**B. Omit biological characterization.** A drug directed at a particular disease process cannot be fairly evaluated if that process is absent in some participants.
**C. Confirm the biology.** Appropriate biomarkers align trial enrollment with the disease mechanism the drug is designed to affect.
**D. Assume other syndromes have the same pathology.** Other dementia syndromes may overlap clinically or have mixed pathology. Their labels cannot establish the same molecular target.

q: When counseling a family about symptomatic medication for Alzheimer disease, which statement best reflects the evidence described in Hazzard?
o: In mild cognitive impairment, acetylcholinesterase inhibitors delay progression to Alzheimer dementia.
In early Alzheimer disease, memantine has sufficient evidence to recommend routine treatment.
In established Alzheimer dementia, acetylcholinesterase inhibitors are used for stability or slower decline.
In moderate-to-severe Alzheimer disease, combined treatment produces better outcomes than either agent alone.
explanation:
Cholinesterase inhibitors provide modest symptomatic benefits in established Alzheimer dementia. **Maintaining everyday abilities or slowing decline relative to the untreated course is a reasonable treatment goal**, with individual review for tolerability and meaningful function.

**A. Prevent conversion from MCI.** Cholinesterase inhibitors have not reliably delayed progression of MCI to Alzheimer dementia.
**B. Routine memantine for early disease.** Its established indication is moderate-to-severe Alzheimer dementia. Evidence does not support routine use in mild disease.
**C. Cholinesterase inhibitors for established dementia.** Discuss small average benefits rather than promising a noticeable improvement or a plateau in every patient.
**D. Combination is superior to either drug alone.** One moderate-to-severe trial found modest cognitive and ADL gains with memantine added to continued donepezil. DOMINO-AD found no significant added benefit over continued donepezil alone. Consistent superiority to both monotherapies has not been shown.

q: Which patient group matches the FDA-approved indication for memantine (Namenda) stated in Hazzard 8e?
o: Patients diagnosed with Alzheimer disease of any severity
Patients diagnosed with moderate to severe Alzheimer disease
Patients diagnosed with the mild cognitive impairment syndrome
Patients diagnosed with Alzheimer disease of mild severity
explanation:
Memantine reduces excessive NMDA receptor activity and is a symptomatic medication. The approved indication specifies Alzheimer dementia and a particular severity range.

**Moderate-to-severe Alzheimer dementia** is the patient group matching that indication.

**A. Alzheimer disease at any severity.** This would extend the indication to mild disease and earlier biological stages.
**B. Moderate-to-severe Alzheimer disease.** At this stage memantine can offer modest benefits in cognition, daily activities or behavior.
**C. Mild cognitive impairment.** MCI retains functional independence. Memantine has no established preventive indication for this syndrome.
**D. Mild Alzheimer disease.** Mild dementia falls earlier than the approved severity range for memantine.

q: What is the most common initial clinical presentation of Alzheimer disease?
o: Initial symptoms dominated by a deficit in executive function
Initial symptoms dominated by a deficit in visuospatial abilities
Initial symptoms dominated by slowly progressive recent-event memory loss
Initial symptoms dominated by a deficit in language abilities
explanation:
The usual first manifestation of Alzheimer disease is difficulty learning or retaining recent events. Relatives may notice repeated questions or forgotten conversations while older memories remain accessible.

**Slowly progressive recent-event memory loss** is the most common initial presentation.

**A. Executive dysfunction first.** Difficulty planning or judging can lead a less common nonamnestic presentation.
**B. Visuospatial impairment first.** An initial problem recognizing objects or navigating space is possible, but is less frequent than amnestic onset.
**C. Progressive recent-memory loss first.** Forgetting newly learned information over months or years gives the characteristic early history.
**D. Language impairment first.** Word-finding difficulty or a language-led syndrome can occur early in some patients, but it is not the usual first pattern.

q: According to Hazzard, how are neuropsychiatric symptoms in dementia associated with disease progression and caregiver burden?
o: Faster disease progression and greater caregiver burden
Faster disease progression and lower caregiver burden
Slower disease progression and greater caregiver burden
Slower disease progression and lower caregiver burden
explanation:
Behavioral and psychiatric symptoms change the demands of caring for a person with dementia. **They are associated with faster disease progression and greater caregiver burden**.

**A. Faster progression and more burden.** Symptoms can disrupt sleep, cooperation and daily care while marking a poorer course.
**B. Faster progression and less burden.** Wandering or aggression commonly requires closer supervision.
**C. Slower progression and more burden.** The burden fits but the observed course is generally worse.
**D. Slower progression and less burden.** Both directions misrepresent the association.

Delirium
Generalized anxiety disorder

q: An older adult with dementia develops irritability and anxiety. Which approach best reflects the presentation of depression in dementia described by Hazzard?
o: Include agitation, irritability, and anxiety in the assessment of depression in dementia.
Favor a separate psychiatric disorder when new depressive symptoms emerge during established dementia.
Use poor concentration and anhedonia as the principal features distinguishing depression from dementia.
Use the presentation in cognitively intact older adults as the main pattern for recognizing depression.
explanation:
**Depression in dementia** may be missed when clinicians expect the presentation seen in cognitively intact older adults. Hazzard notes that "depression in dementia is more likely to present with agitation, irritability, and anxiety." Poor concentration, memory problems, and anhedonia overlap with dementia-related deficits and apathy; this overlap explains why recognition requires attention to the broader depressive presentation rather than treating one overlapping symptom as decisive (p. 923; final application is an inference from that overlap).

**A. Include agitation, irritability, and anxiety in the assessment of depression in dementia.** Correct, these are specifically described presentations of depression in dementia, so considering them helps avoid missing a depressive syndrome (p. 923).
**B. Favor a separate psychiatric disorder when new depressive symptoms emerge during established dementia.** Wrong, new psychiatric symptoms in dementia are more likely related to the underlying dementia than to a separate concurrent psychiatric illness; that proposed default attribution is unsupported (p. 923).
**C. Use poor concentration and anhedonia as the principal features distinguishing depression from dementia.** Wrong, these symptoms overlap with dementia-related cognitive deficits and apathy; treating them as distinguishing features does not resolve the diagnostic overlap (p. 923; application is an inference).
**D. Use the presentation in cognitively intact older adults as the main pattern for recognizing depression.** Wrong, the page warns that depressive presentations can differ considerably from those in people with normal cognition, which is a reason depression goes undetected (p. 923).

q: The MIND at Home study found unmet care needs in nearly all community-dwelling dementia patients. Which care plan best follows the response Hazzard recommends?
o: Support safe surroundings, daily activities and physical and mental health
Support medical treatment while leaving home safety to a later crisis
Support physical care while setting aside meaningful daily activities
Support the patient directly while excluding the caregiver from planning
explanation:
**Unmet dementia-care needs** extend beyond medical treatment to safety, daily activities and caregiver support. Hazzard directs teams to "work with the patient and caregiver" and to "provide a safe environment that maximizes the patient’s physical and cognitive abilities". The point is to preserve function and dignity through coordinated support in everyday life, rather than respond only to a medical crisis (p. 924).

**A. Support safe surroundings, daily activities and physical and mental health.** Correct, this addresses the domains the chapter identifies and uses the patient and caregiver together to preserve abilities and dignity (p. 924).
**B. Support medical treatment while leaving home safety to a later crisis.** Wrong, home safety is an explicit care-team responsibility, so waiting for a crisis leaves one of the common unmet needs unaddressed (p. 924).
**C. Support physical care while setting aside meaningful daily activities.** Wrong, the recommended environment includes activities and socialization; removing meaningful activity leaves part of the care goal unmet (p. 924).
**D. Support the patient directly while excluding the caregiver from planning.** Wrong, the chapter explicitly includes the caregiver in the team response; excluding that person omits a partner whose needs and involvement also matter (p. 924).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th ed., p. 924.

Increase the antipsychotic dose further and continue treatment despite the lack of significant benefit.

Continue the same antipsychotic unchanged for several more months before considering withdrawal.

Antipsychotic treatment for dementia-related agitation needs a demonstrable target response. **Taper and withdraw an ineffective four-week trial**, reassessing symptoms at least monthly during taper.

**A. Taper with monitoring.** Record whether agitation recurs as medication exposure falls.
**B. Escalate despite failure.** Additional exposure increases risk without evidence of meaningful response.
**C. Long-acting injection.** There is no separate chronic psychotic indication to justify prolonged exposure.
**D. Continue unchanged.** Several more months would prolong an ineffective trial.

q: Which statement best describes parkinsonism and its causes?
o: Parkinsonism describes a syndrome for which Parkinson disease is the most common cause.
Parkinsonism describes a syndrome most commonly caused by structural lesions of the brain.
Parkinsonism describes a syndrome in which bradykinesia is less central than the other motor signs.
Parkinsonism describes a syndrome whose causes become less common as people grow older.
explanation:
Parkinsonism describes a pattern of movement abnormalities centered on bradykinesia. Rest tremor, rigidity and impaired postural reflexes can accompany the slowness.

**Parkinson disease is the most common cause of parkinsonism.** A patient can also acquire the same motor pattern from a medication, a structural lesion or another neurodegenerative disorder.

**A. Parkinson disease is the most common cause.** Recognizing the syndrome is the first step. The course, exposures and examination then help identify its cause.
**B. Structural lesions are most common.** Stroke, tumors and hydrocephalus are secondary causes and account for fewer cases than Parkinson disease.
**C. Bradykinesia is less central.** Slowness of movement is the central motor feature even when tremor is subtle or absent.
**D. Causes become less common with age.** Most disorders causing parkinsonism become more frequent with advancing age.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 935–936.

q: At the onset of Parkinson motor symptoms, substantial dopaminergic terminal loss is already present. Which pattern distinguishes this denervation from normal aging in Hazzard?
o: Parkinson disease produces milder and more diffuse loss than normal aging
Parkinson disease preferentially affects anterior and ventral rather than posterior regions
Parkinson disease preferentially affects posterior and dorsal putaminal regions
Parkinson disease and normal aging have similar diffuse regional patterns
explanation:
Dopaminergic nerve terminals in the striatum decline with normal aging, but the location and degree of loss differ in Parkinson disease. At the onset of motor symptoms, denervation in the posterior putamen is already substantial.

**Parkinson disease preferentially affects the posterior and dorsal putamen.** This concentration of injury distinguishes it from the milder, more diffuse loss of normal aging.

**A. Milder and more diffuse disease-related loss.** That description fits aging. Symptomatic Parkinson disease produces much greater local loss.
**B. Anterior and ventral predominance.** These regions are relatively less affected than the posterior and dorsal motor putamen.
**C. Posterior and dorsal predominance.** The distribution involves the putaminal region important for the speed and precision of movement.
**D. Similar diffuse patterns.** Aging and Parkinson disease both affect dopamine terminals, but their regional patterns and severity differ.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 938.

q: In the Braak model, which stage corresponds to nigral involvement and the onset of motor symptoms of PD?
o: Stage 1
Stage 5
Stage 3
Stage 2
explanation:
The Braak model orders Lewy pathology by the regions it reaches as Parkinson disease evolves. Early changes in olfactory and lower brainstem structures can precede the first motor signs.

**Stage 3 is the proposed transition to nigral involvement and motor symptoms.** Degeneration of the substantia nigra disrupts the dopamine supply needed for normal movement.

**A. Stage 1.** This is an early premotor stage involving lower brainstem and olfactory regions.
**B. Stage 5.** Later cortical involvement is associated with cognitive impairment, after nigral disease is already present.
**C. Stage 3.** Lewy pathology reaches the substantia nigra in this model, corresponding to the emergence of parkinsonian motor features.
**D. Stage 2.** This is also a premotor stage, in which sleep or autonomic symptoms may be evident before nigral motor involvement.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 939.

q: A patient with bradykinesia is being assessed for Parkinson disease. Which interpretation of an adjunctive finding is supported by Hazzard?
o: A positive DaTscan distinguishes Parkinson disease from multiple system atrophy.
A positive DaTscan supports loss of nigrostriatal dopaminergic nerve terminals.
A positive levodopa response identifies Parkinson disease rather than atypical parkinsonism.
A tremor that increases during handwriting supports Parkinson disease rather than essential tremor.
explanation:
Dopamine transporter imaging assesses whether striatal dopaminergic terminals have been lost. Neither an abnormal scan nor an improvement with levodopa uniquely identifies the cause of a parkinsonian syndrome.

**An abnormal DaTscan supports nigrostriatal dopaminergic terminal loss.** It can corroborate degenerative parkinsonism when the examination is uncertain.

**A. The scan separates Parkinson disease from multiple system atrophy.** Both disorders can reduce striatal uptake, so their clinical patterns still matter.
**B. The scan supports terminal loss.** Reduced tracer uptake reflects diminished presynaptic dopamine transporter signal in the striatum.
**C. Levodopa response uniquely identifies Parkinson disease.** A substantial sustained response supports idiopathic disease, but some patients with multiple system atrophy or Lewy body dementia also improve.
**D. Writing-induced tremor favors Parkinson disease.** Tremor increasing during a voluntary task is more typical of essential tremor. Parkinsonian tremor usually predominates at rest.

q: An older adult has a fall without physical injury but becomes afraid of falling again. Which consequence of this fear is described in Hazzard?
o: Avoidance of daily activities helps preserve mobility during recovery.
Lack of physical injury protects against subsequent fear-related frailty.
Restriction of daily activities improves balance by increasing rest.
Avoidance of daily activities reduces mobility and contributes to frailty.
explanation:
Falls can have consequences even when there is no fracture or soft-tissue injury. **Fear may lead to activity avoidance, reduced mobility and increasing frailty**.

**A. Avoidance preserves mobility.** Loss of daily movement can reduce conditioning and undermine function.
**B. No injury protects against frailty.** Fear-driven inactivity can occur in someone whose physical examination is normal.
**C. Restriction improves balance.** Rest does not provide the repeated weight shifts and walking practice needed to maintain stability.
**D. Avoidance reduces mobility.** Ask what the patient has stopped doing and address the loss of confidence alongside physical risks.

q: An older resident falls without sustaining a physical injury, then becomes afraid of falling again. Which pathway explains why this event still warrants attention?
o: Post-fall anxiety increases participation in daily activities and improves confidence in balance.
Fear-driven avoidance of daily activities reduces mobility and contributes to increasing frailty.
Preserved physical integrity makes avoidance of daily activities protective against subsequent frailty.
Reduced activity after the fall lowers the subsequent need for institutional support.
explanation:
After an uninjured fall, changes in behavior can still lead to functional decline. **Fear-driven avoidance reduces mobility and can worsen frailty** in a resident who begins giving up routine activities.

**A. Anxiety increases participation.** Fear commonly leads a person to avoid situations perceived as unsafe.
**B. Avoidance impairs mobility.** Less walking and fewer transfers reduce opportunities to maintain strength and balance.
**C. Preserved physical integrity makes avoidance protective.** A normal injury assessment cannot prevent deconditioning from inactivity.
**D. Reduced activity lowers support needs.** Loss of function can increase the assistance required for daily tasks.

q: An older adult avoids usual daily activities because of fear after a fall. Which combination of functional consequences does Hazzard describe?
o: Reduced mobility and increased frailty through activity avoidance
Preserved mobility and increased frailty through activity avoidance
Reduced mobility and decreased frailty through activity avoidance

"the risk of falls is significantly increased within the 24-hour periods following the initiation of an antihypertensive or change in antihypertensive dose." (p636).

q: A robust older adult falls on an icy path, while an older adult with very poor physical abilities falls in a relatively hazard-free home. Which interpretation fits Hazzard?

explanation:

**A. Lower ability tolerates greater demands.** Lower reserve narrows the range of challenges the person can handle safely.
**B. Fewer demands endanger robust walkers.** An easier environment usually reduces challenge for any given level of ability.
**C. Ability loses importance with greater demands.** Greater demands make balance and recovery capacity particularly relevant.
**D. Ability and environment interact.** A prevention plan can improve the person's capacity, reduce hazards or address both.

q: How far does a patient walk during the Timed Up and Go (TUG) test?

1.35 meters outward, then return
3 meters outward, then return to the chair
No walking distance: only repeated chair rises
explanation:
The **Timed Up and Go** samples a sequence of mobility tasks: standing, walking, turning and sitting. The patient must “walk 3 meters at normal pace and with usual assistive devices,” then turn and return to the chair; shortening the walk or omitting it changes the task being assessed (last clause is an inference from the protocol, p. 637).

**A. 18 cm outward, then return.** Wrong, an outward walk of only 18 cm does not perform the specified walking segment and would change the test protocol (p. 637).
**B. 1.35 meters outward, then return.** Wrong, 1.35 meters shortens the outward segment below the specified 3 meters, so it is not the TUG described in the chapter (p. 637).
**C. 3 meters outward, then return to the chair.** Correct, it includes the specified outward walk and return; timing also includes rising, turning and sitting (p. 637).

q: Per UK NICE guidance, which hospital patients should automatically undergo a falls risk assessment?

**A. Patients aged 65 or older after a documented inpatient fall, plus all patients aged 50–64.** Wrong, a previous inpatient fall is not required for patients aged 65 or older. Patients aged 50–64 need an underlying condition placing them at risk; the rule does not include everyone in that age range (p. 637, Assessment – Hospitals).
**B. Patients aged 65 or older with abnormal balance testing, plus those aged 50–64 after a fall.** Wrong, abnormal balance testing is not required before assessing the older group. The younger group qualifies through an underlying risk condition, such as recent stroke, rather than only after a fall (p. 637).
**C. All patients aged 65 or older, plus those aged 50–64 with an underlying risk condition.** Correct, the hospital rule is age 65 or older, or age 50–64 with an underlying risk condition. Assessment is multifactorial and leads to individualized interventions (p. 637).
**D. Patients aged 65 or older taking psychoactive drugs, plus those aged 50–64 with an MMSE below 17.** Wrong, psychoactive medication use is not a prerequisite for the older hospital group. The MMSE threshold below 17 appears in the residential-care fall screen, not the hospital eligibility rule (p. 637).

q: After completing a CaHFRiS fall screen for a care-home resident, which use of the findings is most appropriate?
o: Focus the subsequent assessment on cognition rather than the other recorded risk factors.

Use the combined score to establish the underlying cause of the resident's cognitive impairment.
explanation:
The **CaHFRiS Fall Screen** combines cognitive, behavioral, balance, mobility, medication and falls-history information. Its usefulness is not limited to assigning a probability: the identified risk factors can help direct interventions to the particular resident's problems (p637).
"While described as a fall risk screen, this tool assists in identifying important explanatory risk factors for falls that may be amenable to targeted interventions." (p637).

**A. Focus the subsequent assessment on cognition rather than the other recorded risk factors.** Wrong, cognition is one item among several; limiting assessment to it misses balance, medication and falls-history factors included in the screen (p637).
**B. Record the estimated probability of falling without using the individual items for care planning.** Wrong, the text says the screen identifies explanatory factors amenable to targeted interventions, so a risk estimate is not the end of the process (p637).
**C. Use the identified contributors to guide targeted assessment and fall-prevention interventions.** Correct, the screen helps identify contributors to falling that may be addressed with targeted interventions (p637).
**D. Use the combined score to establish the underlying cause of the resident's cognitive impairment.** Wrong, the screen concerns future falls in care-home residents, not a diagnosis of a particular dementia cause (p637).

explanation:

**A. Prioritizing low-challenge activity rather than challenging balance tasks.** Wrong, the review found greater effects from high-challenge balance work; minimizing that challenge omits a feature associated with greater benefit (p. 638).

**C. Requiring group delivery rather than allowing an individual program.** Wrong, exercise was effective whether delivered in a group or individually; group delivery is not the deciding requirement (p. 638).
**D. Providing challenging balance tasks with sufficient weekly exercise.** Correct, challenging balance work and three or more prescribed hours per week were associated with greater reductions in falls (p. 638).

q: Pressure injuries are especially common in older adults. Which principle should guide prevention after initial risk screening?

Use wound location alone to establish a pressure-related etiology
Reserve prevention for patients who are confined to lying in bed

explanation:
Pressure injury reflects the interaction between mechanical exposure and the tissue's ability to tolerate it. Screening identifies who needs a more specific assessment and prevention plan.

**Identify the individual's risks and act on them.** Address mobility, positioning, skin moisture, nutrition, perfusion and pressure from devices as appropriate.

**A. Targeted assessment and prevention.** A patient who cannot turn needs help unloading bony prominences. Reduced intake or excess moisture requires different additional measures.
**B. Diagnosis from location alone.** Pressure wounds often occur over bone, but ischemic, neuropathic or moisture-related lesions can occur nearby.
**C. Prevention confined to bedbound people.** Sitting, medical devices and prolonged surgical positioning can also expose tissue to pressure.

Advanced chronological age

q: Why can a pressure injury cause substantial deep muscle damage before skin breakdown becomes visible?

Increased local temperature reduces tissue oxygen requirements during compression.
explanation:

**B. High metabolic demand and deformation.** Reduced oxygen availability and mechanical distortion work together to injure muscle cells.
**C. Reperfusion ends all injury.** Restoring flow can generate oxygen free radicals that cause further endothelial damage.
**D. Heat lowers oxygen needs.** Higher tissue temperature raises metabolic demand and can intensify hypoxic injury during compression.

q: After prolonged pressure over a bony prominence, an older adult’s skin is still intact. Which interpretation best reflects the tissue injury process described by Hazzard?

Local inflammatory edema can improve arteriolar circulation in the injured tissue.
Reperfusion can protect the endothelium by reducing oxygen-free radical release.
explanation:
The visible skin surface can lag behind injury at the bone–muscle interface. Inflammation and edema can begin days before tissue loss becomes apparent.

**Muscle injury can precede visible skin breakdown.** Offload and examine the area again after a significant pressure exposure, even when the initial surface is intact.

**A. Deep damage before surface loss.** Muscle is metabolically active and vulnerable to deformation, so intact skin does not guarantee intact underlying tissue.
**B. Ischemic muscle resists deformation.** Oxygen deprivation makes muscle more susceptible to deformation injury.
**C. Edema improves circulation.** Rising interstitial pressure impedes arteriolar and lymphatic flow and can worsen local swelling and ischemia.
**D. Reperfusion reduces free radicals.** Reoxygenation can generate free radicals and add endothelial injury after the load is removed.

**D. 40 percent.** The residual tensile strength is well under half of native tissue strength, helping explain recurrent injury under load.

explanation:
**Urinary incontinence** is common in older adults and becomes more prevalent with increasing frailty. q: During bladder filling, what immediate relationship between bladder pressure and outlet resistance permits urinary leakage?

Bladder pressure exceeds outlet resistance while urine is being stored
explanation:
During bladder filling, urethral closure must withstand the pressure inside the bladder. **Leakage occurs when bladder pressure exceeds outlet resistance**, whether from a detrusor contraction, abdominal strain or inadequate closure.

**A. Pressure below resistance.** The outlet can retain urine under this relationship.
**B. Low pressure with greater resistance.** This favors continued storage and continence.
**C. Resistance above pressure during a contraction.** A contraction may cause urgency, but leakage requires that it overcome the outlet.
**D. Pressure exceeds resistance.** Once the outlet can no longer contain the filling bladder, urine escapes.

q: Which class of antihypertensive is classically linked to stress incontinence via a chronic cough?

Alpha-adrenergic blockers
Diuretics

**Stress incontinence** is leakage accompanying increased intra-abdominal pressure, including during coughing. Table 47-4 links ACE inhibitors to “Cough precipitating stress incontinence,” explaining the drug-to-symptom chain in this stem (p. 703).

q: A woman performs a cough stress test while standing with a comfortably full bladder. Which observation documents stress urinary incontinence?

Urine leakage occurs at the same time as the cough
explanation:
A cough stress test reproduces a sudden rise in abdominal pressure while the bladder contains enough urine to detect leakage. **Leakage synchronous with the cough** corroborates stress urinary incontinence.

**A. Leakage seconds later.** Delay suggests a cough-triggered detrusor contraction rather than immediate outlet failure.
**B. Sustained voiding after the cough.** A sustained stream suggests initiation of bladder contraction.
**C. No leakage with a nearly empty bladder.** Low bladder volume reduces test sensitivity and cannot document stress leakage.
**D. Simultaneous leakage.** Immediate loss during the pressure spike is the characteristic stress-test finding.
