q: In which direction is clinicians' survival estimate commonly biased?
o: Toward overestimation by a factor of 3 to 5
Clinical estimates are entirely uncorrelated with actual survival
Toward underestimation by a factor of 3 to 5
No systematic bias is described
explanation:
Clinicians tend to overestimate survival by a factor of 3 to 5 (p1051).

C. Toward underestimation by a factor of 3 to 5: The stated direction is overestimation (p1051).
D. No systematic bias is described: The book describes numerous biases, particularly overestimation (p1051).
B. Clinical estimates are entirely uncorrelated with actual survival: The book says judgment-based estimates are correlated with survival despite bias (p1051).
chapterTitle: Palliative Care and Special Management Issues

q: Why does adequate control of acute postoperative pain matter for an older adult’s longer-term recovery?
o: Poorly controlled pain may protect against chronic pain by reducing mobility demands.
Poorly controlled pain may shorten admission by limiting excessive postoperative activity.
Appropriate pain control may help prevent chronic pain and pain-related mobility limitations.
Appropriate pain control may improve comfort while increasing the later risk of chronic pain.
explanation:
**Acute pain control** matters beyond immediate comfort, because poorly controlled postoperative pain is associated with limited mobility and prolonged admission (p. 1055). The chapter adds that “acute pain that is appropriately managed during the perioperative period may help prevent the development of chronic pain.” (p. 1055).

**A. Poorly controlled pain may protect against chronic pain by reducing mobility demands.** Wrong, poor control is associated with limited mobility and increased chronic-pain risk; pain-related immobility is not described as protective (p. 1055).
**B. Poorly controlled pain may shorten admission by limiting excessive postoperative activity.** Wrong, poor control is associated with prolonged hospital stays, contradicting the proposed shorter admission (p. 1055).
**C. Appropriate pain control may help prevent chronic pain and pain-related mobility limitations.** Correct, the page reports adverse mobility consequences of poor control and possible prevention of chronic pain with appropriate perioperative management (p. 1055).
**D. Appropriate pain control may improve comfort while increasing the later risk of chronic pain.** Wrong, the stated later effect is possible prevention of chronic pain, rather than increased chronic-pain risk (p. 1055).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8e, pp. 1055.

q: Which mechanism defines neuropathic pain in Hazzard, rather than nociceptive pain?
o: Activation of pain receptors by local tissue inflammation
A lesion or disease affecting the somatosensory system
Activation of pain receptors by mechanical tissue distortion
Activation of pain receptors by tissue injury after trauma
explanation:
Neuropathic pain arises when the nervous system carrying somatic sensation is damaged or diseased. **A lesion or disease of the somatosensory system is the defining mechanism**.

**A. Local inflammation.** Inflamed tissue stimulates nociceptors and causes nociceptive pain.
**B. Somatosensory lesion.** Peripheral nerve injury or central sensory pathway disease can generate pain.
**C. Mechanical distortion.** Pressure or stretching of intact tissue activates nociceptors.
**D. Tissue trauma.** Injury can cause nociceptive pain unless it also damages the sensory nervous system.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1056.

q: About what fraction of Medicare Part D beneficiaries received an opioid prescription in a 2016 analysis?
o: A quarter
One in three
explanation:
One in three Medicare Part D beneficiaries received an opioid prescription in the 2016 analysis (p1060).

A. A quarter: This is the share of vertebral compression fractures resulting from falls (p1066); the requested value is one in three (p1060).
C. 60%: This is arthritis/chronic joint pain prevalence at age 65 or older (p1066); the requested value is one in three (p1060).
B. 7% to 10%: This is neuropathic pain prevalence (p1056); the requested value is one in three (p1060).
retiredReason: US health-system policy (Medicare, Medicaid, PACE, US federal law or agency); not part of the Israeli exam.

q: How does opioid-induced hyperalgesia present clinically, in contrast to opioid tolerance?
o: Improving pain with increasing opioid doses
Tolerance alone, with no increase in pain on dose escalation
Increased levels of pain with increased doses of opioids
Reduced sensitivity to painful stimuli
explanation:
Opioid-induced hyperalgesia often produces increased pain with increased opioid doses, unlike tolerance alone (p1061).

A. Improving pain with increasing opioid doses: The distinguishing pattern is worsening, not improvement, with higher doses (p1061).
B. Tolerance alone, with no increase in pain on dose escalation: The book distinguishes simple loss of effect from the worsening pain of hyperalgesia (p1061).
D. Reduced sensitivity to painful stimuli: Hyperalgesia is increased sensitivity to painful stimuli (p1061).

q: A patient with facet-mediated pain obtains 80% pain relief after a diagnostic medial-branch nerve block. What is the clinical significance of this response?
o: It argues against the medial branch as a relevant target for a subsequent intervention.
It supports considering radiofrequency denervation of the medial branch for longer-lasting pain relief.
It supports vertebral augmentation as the next treatment for the facet-mediated pain.
It supports repeating diagnostic testing while ruling out a longer-lasting nerve procedure.
explanation:
A medial branch block tests whether facet-joint afferents contribute to back pain. **An 80% reduction supports considering medial branch radiofrequency denervation** for potentially longer relief.

**A. Argues against the target.** Marked response supports involvement of the blocked nerve.
**B. Consider denervation.** A strong temporary response helps select a patient for a longer-acting procedure.
**C. Vertebral augmentation.** This treats selected compression fractures, not facet-mediated pain.
**D. Rule out further nerve treatment.** The diagnostic result supports evaluation for targeted treatment.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1066.

q: In an older adult with a vertebral compression fracture, which presentation supports considering vertebroplasty or kyphoplasty, rather than representing a listed contraindication?
o: An acutely painful vertebral fracture in a patient with an existing coagulopathy.
An acutely painful burst fracture with retropulsed bone on the spinal imaging.
An acutely painful vertebral fracture persisting despite analgesics, bracing, and physical therapy.
An acutely painful vertebral fracture with vertebral height loss greater than 66%.
explanation:
A vertebral compression fracture can remain a source of disabling focal pain after initial treatment. **Consider vertebroplasty or kyphoplasty when pain attributable to the acute fracture persists despite analgesics, bracing and physical therapy**, after assessing anatomy and risk.

**A. Existing coagulopathy.** Significant uncorrected bleeding risk argues against proceeding until it is addressed.
**B. Burst fracture with retropulsed bone.** A fragment in the spinal canal can threaten neural structures and requires a different assessment.
**C. Persistent pain after conservative care.** Severe focal symptoms that match the fracture on imaging support discussing augmentation in selected patients.
**D. More than 66% vertebral height loss.** The markedly flattened body may leave too little space for safe access and cement containment or for restoring height. This calls for individualized specialist assessment and is generally a relative technical limitation.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1066. ACR practice guideline for percutaneous vertebroplasty, relative contraindications.

q: Which description best explains the process underlying osteoarthritic joint pain?
o: A stable cartilage lesion accompanied by preserved structure in other joint tissues.
A dynamic repair process that restores damaged cartilage while preserving joint architecture.
A dynamic imbalance between repair and destruction involving multiple joint tissues.
A localized synovial process accompanied by preserved adjacent bone and ligament structure.
explanation:
Osteoarthritis affects the whole joint, with changing relationships among cartilage, bone, synovium, ligaments and capsule. **An imbalance between tissue repair and destruction underlies the process**.

**A. Stable cartilage defect.** OA is dynamic and includes tissues beyond cartilage.
**B. Repair restores architecture.** Repair can be inadequate and remodeling can distort joint architecture.
**C. Whole-joint imbalance.** Different tissues participate in structural change and pain generation.
**D. Synovium alone.** Bone and connective tissue abnormalities also contribute.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1066.

q: A clinician is comparing intra-articular injection studies for knee osteoarthritis. Which statement about the preparations and evidence is consistent with Hazzard?
o: Hyaluronic acid preparations differ in injection schedules but share their origin and molecular weight.
Platelet-rich plasma preparations vary in the number of centrifugations, changing the platelet concentration delivered.
Corticosteroid injections offer benefits that are better established over the long term than the short term.
Platelet-rich plasma injections use a depot steroid mixed with a local anesthetic to promote joint healing.
explanation:
Intra-articular OA preparations differ in composition and the duration of their evidence. **Platelet-rich plasma preparations can deliver different platelet concentrations**, limiting comparisons between studies.

**A. Identical hyaluronic acid products.** Preparations differ in origin and molecular weight as well as schedules.
**B. Variable platelet concentration.** Variation in preparation affects the concentration administered.
**C. Steroids best proven long term.** Pain relief is better established over the short term.
**D. PRP as a steroid mixture.** PRP is a platelet-containing blood product, distinct from a depot corticosteroid injection.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1067.

q: Does cardiomyocyte loss leave uniformly smaller surviving cells?
o: Yes - all surviving cells become uniformly smaller
No - surviving myocytes enlarge and become more variable in size
No - the largest surviving cells are the least vulnerable to stress
No - surviving cells enlarge but become uniform in size
explanation:
Surviving cardiac myocytes increase in size and become more variable in size as cardiomyocytes are lost with aging (p1116).

A. Yes - all surviving cells become uniformly smaller: The book describes increased and more variable size (p1116).
D. No - surviving cells enlarge but become uniform in size: Size variability increases rather than disappears (p1116).
C. No - the largest surviving cells are the least vulnerable to stress: The largest cells are described as most vulnerable (p1116).

q: Why can a senile/sigmoid septum complicate echo interpretation?
o: Basal septal thickening is generally evidence of biological aging rather than hypertension
Basal septal thickening is a potential confounder in diagnosing hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
Basal septal thickening is useful for excluding hypertrophic cardiomyopathy in older patients
This septal pattern is defined by thinning of the basal ventricular septum
explanation:
A sigmoid septum is disproportionate thickening of the basal ventricular septum seen in some older adults. **It can mimic hypertrophic cardiomyopathy on echocardiography**.

**A. Biological aging rather than hypertension.** Hypertension can contribute to the appearance.
**B. Confounds HCM diagnosis.** Interpret thickness and distribution with clinical findings, gradients and family history.
**C. Excludes HCM.** Basal thickening alone neither proves nor excludes cardiomyopathy.
**D. Basal thinning.** The morphology involves thickening, not thinning.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1119.

q: Does aortic sclerosis mean significant valvular obstruction?
o: No - aortic sclerosis is associated with a lower cardiovascular mortality risk
No - the valve thickens without significant hemodynamic dysfunction
Yes - progression to clinical stenosis is the defining feature of aortic sclerosis
Yes - thickened leaflets generally indicate significant hemodynamic obstruction
explanation:
Aortic sclerosis is leaflet thickening with little hemodynamic effect. **It does not imply significant obstruction**, although it marks increased cardiovascular risk.

**A. Lower cardiovascular mortality.** Sclerosis is associated with higher, not lower, cardiovascular mortality.
**B. Thickening without major dysfunction.** Flow measurements distinguish sclerosis from hemodynamically significant stenosis.
**C. Progression defines sclerosis.** Some valves progress, but progression is not required for the diagnosis.
**D. Leaflet thickness proves obstruction.** Assess gradients and valve opening before diagnosing stenosis.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1119.

q: Describe regurgitation compatible with normal aging.
o: Trivial or mild central regurgitation with leaflets appearing normal for age
Severe central regurgitation with leaflets appearing normal for the patient’s age
Trivial or mild central regurgitation with leaflets showing major structural abnormalities
Moderate central regurgitation with leaflets appearing normal for the patient’s age
explanation:
A small central regurgitant jet can occur with age-related valve or annular changes. **Trivial or mild central regurgitation with leaflets normal for age** fits a physiologic aging pattern.

**A. Trivial or mild and normal leaflets.** Both severity and morphology are compatible.
**B. Severe central regurgitation.** Severity warrants assessment for pathology despite a central jet.
**C. Abnormal leaflets.** Major structural disease requires its own explanation even with a small jet.
**D. Moderate central regurgitation.** Moderate leakage exceeds the expected aging pattern.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1120.

q: Is a thin, hypermobile atrial septum the expected aging pattern?
o: No - septal mobility with phasic respiration increases with age
No - the atrial septum thickens and becomes stiffer with age
Yes - a thin hypermobile septum needs no further evaluation in older adults
Yes - a thin hypermobile septum is the expected aging change
explanation:
The atrial septum thickens and stiffens with age; a thin hypermobile septum should prompt further evaluation (p1120).

D. Yes - a thin hypermobile septum is the expected aging change: That finding prompts investigation for aneurysm, PFO, or ASD (p1120).
A. No - septal mobility with phasic respiration increases with age: The book describes reduced mobility (p1120).
C. Yes - a thin hypermobile septum needs no further evaluation in older adults: Color Doppler and agitated-saline contrast evaluation are recommended for this unexpected finding (p1120).

q: Why does faster pulse-wave travel increase cardiac workload?
o: The reflected wave returns only after aortic valve closure and lowers systolic load
The reflected wave delays its return as arteries stiffen
Earlier reflected-wave arrival improves coronary perfusion without affecting LV afterload
Reflected waves return before aortic valve closure, increasing LV afterload
explanation:
Earlier reflected-wave return before aortic valve closure increases LV afterload as arteries stiffen (p1130-1131).

A. The reflected wave returns only after aortic valve closure and lowers systolic load: Return after closure describes the younger-heart timing; aging brings earlier return (p1130-1131).
B. The reflected wave delays its return as arteries stiffen: Stiffening increases pulse-wave velocity and brings earlier return (p1130-1131).
C. Earlier reflected-wave arrival improves coronary perfusion without affecting LV afterload: That benefit is associated with later, diastolic arrival; earlier arrival increases afterload (p1131).

q: What percentage of patients older than 70 with severe symptomatic aortic stenosis were not offered surgery in the cited European study?
explanation:
In the cited European study, 41% of symptomatic severe-AS patients older than 70 were not offered surgery (p1152).

A. 33%: This is the second study of patients older than 75, not the first study of those older than 70 (p1152); the requested value is 41% (p1152).
C. 8.8%: This is overall operative mortality in Medicare outcomes data (p1152); the requested value is 41% (p1152).
D. 6.0%: This is operative mortality in high-volume centers (p1152); the requested value is 41% (p1152).
retiredReason: Number recall from one passage; not exam-style.

q: Why does atrial contraction contribute more to left-ventricular filling in older adults?
o: Enhanced early ventricular filling reduces the need for a late atrial contribution.
A smaller left atrium compensates by reducing resistance to passive ventricular filling.
Improved ventricular compliance shifts filling toward the rapid early-diastolic phase.
Impaired early filling increases reliance on compensatory atrial contraction late in diastole.
explanation:
Aging changes **diastolic filling** because ventricular relaxation and compliance become less favorable. Reduced early filling increases reliance on a more forceful left-atrial contraction later in diastole; the atrium enlarges in response to increased resistance to emptying. This explains the greater importance of the atrial contribution in older adults (p1169).
"Early filling is impaired, and the upstroke of the E-wave is delayed." (p1169).
"To compensate for increased resistance to emptying, the left atrium enlarges." (p1169).

**A. Enhanced early ventricular filling reduces the need for a late atrial contribution.** Wrong, early filling is impaired rather than enhanced, so the atrial contribution becomes more important (p1169).
**B. A smaller left atrium compensates by reducing resistance to passive ventricular filling.** Wrong, the atrium enlarges and contracts more forcefully to compensate; a smaller atrial contribution would not describe the stated adaptation (p1169).
**C. Improved ventricular compliance shifts filling toward the rapid early-diastolic phase.** Wrong, the age-related pattern shifts a greater proportion of filling to late diastole, not toward rapid early filling (p1169).
**D. Impaired early filling increases reliance on compensatory atrial contraction late in diastole.** Correct, this links impaired early filling to the compensatory increase in late atrial contribution (p1169).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th ed., p1169.

q: What proportion of older adults hospitalized for HFPEF with increased LV wall thickness (>12 mm) were found to have wild-type transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis?
explanation:
Wild-type transthyretin amyloidosis was found in 13% of older hospitalized HFPEF patients with LV wall thickness above 12 mm (p1171).

C. 4%: This is the upper reported frequency of transthyretin gene variants in African-Americans (p1171); the requested value is 13% (p1171).
B. 41%: This is the proportion of symptomatic severe-AS patients older than 70 not offered surgery in another study (p1152); the requested value is 13% (p1171).
D. 33%: This is the proportion of symptomatic severe-AS patients older than 75 not offered replacement in another study (p1152); the requested value is 13% (p1171).
retiredReason: Number recall from one passage; not exam-style.

q: What is the single most common precipitant of an acute heart failure exacerbation in a patient with preexisting HF?
o: New-onset or recurrent atrial fibrillation or flutter
Iatrogenic volume overload
Myocardial ischemia or infarction
Nonadherence to medications and/or diet
explanation:
Nonadherence to medications and/or diet is the most common precipitant in preexisting HF and may contribute to as many as two-thirds of exacerbations (p1172).

C. Myocardial ischemia or infarction: These are among the most common cardiac precipitants, but nonadherence is the most common precipitant overall in preexisting HF (p1172).
A. New-onset or recurrent atrial fibrillation or flutter: These are common cardiac precipitants, not the single most common overall precipitant named in this population (p1172).
B. Iatrogenic volume overload: This is an important precipitant in hospitalized patients; nonadherence is the most common overall precipitant (p1172).

q: Why must sacubitril/valsartan (ARNi) initiation be timed carefully relative to a prior ACE inhibitor?
o: The washout is required because ARNi raises potassium more often than ACE inhibitor therapy
No ACE inhibitor washout is required because ARNi therapy cannot cause angioedema
At least a 36-hour ACE-inhibitor washout is needed to mitigate angioedema
Concurrent ACE inhibitor and ARNi therapy is needed to prevent angioedema
explanation:
Transitioning from an ACE inhibitor to ARNi requires at least a 36-hour washout to mitigate angioedema (p1180).

D. Concurrent ACE inhibitor and ARNi therapy is needed to prevent angioedema: The book requires an ACE-inhibitor washout to mitigate angioedema, not concurrent administration (p1180).
B. No ACE inhibitor washout is required because ARNi therapy cannot cause angioedema: ARNi may lead to angioedema and the transition requires a washout (p1180).
A. The washout is required because ARNi raises potassium more often than ACE inhibitor therapy: The book reports lower risk of potassium elevation with ARNi than ACEI and specifies angioedema as the washout rationale (p1180).

q: Frequent right ventricular pacing is associated with increased heart-failure hospitalizations. Which physiologic explanation does Hazzard give for its adverse effects?
o: Improved ventricular synchrony accompanied by progressive chamber enlargement
Reduced functional mitral regurgitation accompanied by improved ejection fraction
Protection from cardiomyopathy as right ventricular pacing becomes more frequent
Ventricular dyssynchrony with adverse remodeling and reduced ejection fraction
explanation:
Right ventricular pacing can activate the ventricles in an abnormal sequence. **Frequent RV pacing may cause dyssynchrony, adverse remodeling and reduced EF**, increasing the risk of HF hospitalization.

**A. Improved synchrony.** Standard RV pacing can make contraction less coordinated.
**B. Less mitral regurgitation and higher EF.** Functional mitral regurgitation can worsen as ventricular function falls.
**C. Protection with greater pacing burden.** The risk of pacing-induced cardiomyopathy increases with frequent RV pacing.
**D. Dyssynchrony and remodeling.** Unequal contraction can promote chamber enlargement and impaired systolic function.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1199.

q: In the AFFIRM trial subgroup analysis of patients older than 70, what happened with antiarrhythmic drug (AAD) therapy?
o: AAD therapy was associated with higher all-cause mortality
AAD therapy was safer than rate control with the same efficacy
AAD therapy was associated with fewer adverse events in older patients
AAD therapy was associated with lower all-cause mortality
explanation:
AAD therapy was associated with higher all-cause mortality (p1201).

D. AAD therapy was associated with lower all-cause mortality: The AFFIRM older-than-70 subgroup had higher, not lower, all-cause mortality with AAD (p1201).
C. AAD therapy was associated with fewer adverse events in older patients: The chapter describes increased adverse events with AAD in older patients, not fewer (p1201).
B. AAD therapy was safer than rate control with the same efficacy: The chapter describes rate control as appearing safer with the same efficacy, and reports higher mortality with AAD in this subgroup (p1201).

q: An older patient with COPD needs long-term inhaled corticosteroids. Which approach to bone risk follows the discussion in Hazzard?
o: Consider osteoporosis prevention because prolonged inhaled therapy is associated with systemic bone effects.
Focus bone prevention on oral steroid courses because inhaled doses are inactivated before systemic exposure.
Base bone-risk assessment on inhaler technique because systemic risk is independent of duration of treatment.
Defer osteoporosis prevention at higher inhaled doses because accelerated bone loss occurs at lower exposure.
explanation:
**Inhaled corticosteroids can have systemic adverse effects.** The absorbed fraction that escapes inactivation contributes to those effects, and risk depends on dose, duration, and patient factors. q: What FEV1 threshold is used as a red flag for advanced COPD needing palliative-care consideration?

**A. FEV1 less than 50% predicted.** Wrong, this broader threshold includes obstruction that does not meet the very-severe threshold in the cited passage; it is not the specific red flag asked about (p. 1262).
**B. FEV1 and diffusing capacity (DLCO) less than 25% of predicted.** Wrong, requiring both FEV1 and DLCO to be this low adds a restriction absent from the palliative-care criterion; such patients may warrant consideration, but this is not the stated screening threshold (p. 1262).
**C. FEV1 < 30% predicted or FEV1 Z-score < –2.55.** Correct, this gives the two alternative measures of very severe obstruction used as a warning of potentially uncontrolled symptoms, while still requiring broader assessment (p. 1262).
**D. FEV1 alone is sufficient to identify everyone who benefits from palliative care.** Wrong, this would miss patients whose palliative needs are evident through symptoms, gas exchange or functional decline; the chapter explicitly says FEV1 alone is insufficient (p. 1262).

q: What makes podocyte loss important in the proposed sclerosis mechanism?

explanation:

Clinical tumors generally emerge after multiple cellular changes over time. **Aging allows damaging events to accumulate alongside changes in repair, telomeres and the microenvironment**.

**B. Accumulated cellular events.** Time permits sequential changes and interactions with the surrounding tissue.

q: Why is ECOG performance status alone considered insufficient in geriatric oncology?

CGA primarily duplicates the functional information from ECOG performance status in older patients with a good ECOG score

Hazzard says CGA “can uncover problems that would not otherwise be identified by routine history and physical or by the traditional oncology performance status tools”; this remains useful even with good ECOG performance status (pp. 1387–1388).

**A. CGA generally contributes less to functional assessment than ECOG performance status in older patients who otherwise appear fit.** Wrong, it understates CGA’s added contribution and risks missing clinically relevant vulnerabilities in patients who appear fit (pp. 1387–1388).
**B. CGA primarily duplicates the functional information from ECOG performance status in older patients with a good ECOG score.** Wrong, it treats the assessments as redundant, although CGA identifies problems that routine performance-status assessment can miss (p. 1388).

o: Substitute conventional oncology performance status for geriatric assessment when planning care for older patients.

"These studies demonstrate that CGA-guided interventions can in fact lead to decreased treatment toxicity and improve key outcomes for older patients with cancer." (p. 1388).
"It can uncover problems that would not otherwise be identified by routine history and physical or by the traditional oncology performance status tools." (p. 1388).

**D. It has a higher perforation risk than colonoscopy in older adults.** Wrong, the chapter reports greater perforation risk with colonoscopy; sigmoidoscopy’s important disadvantage here is coverage, despite its lower complication risk (p. 1439).

Source: Hazzard's Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th ed., pp. 1439.

q: When considering whether to stop colorectal-cancer screening in an older adult, which approach is most consistent with the chapter?
o: Use age-based average survival without adjustment for chronic disease or functional status.
Base the decision on the number of diagnoses without considering their severity or prognosis.
Continue screening despite a prognosis shorter than the expected progression time of a polyp.
Compare individualized life expectancy with the time needed for polyp progression to cancer.
explanation:
Decisions about **stopping colorectal-cancer screening** should compare remaining life expectancy with the time needed for a polyp to progress to cancer. The chapter also requires prognosis to account for chronic disease and functional status. Inference: when expected survival is shorter than the progression interval, screening is less likely to deliver its intended future benefit (p1440).
"This estimate must be adjusted for the number and severity of chronic diseases affecting the individual, as well as his or her functional status." (p1440).
"It may be reasonable to discontinue screening when life expectancy is shorter than the time a polyp progresses to a cancer, that is, 5 to 10 years." (p1440).

**A. Use age-based average survival without adjustment for chronic disease or functional status.** Wrong, age-based averages must be adjusted for chronic disease and functional status; chronological age alone does not supply an individualized prognosis (p1440).
**B. Base the decision on the number of diagnoses without considering their severity or prognosis.** Wrong, the presence of disease matters through its severity and effect on prognosis, not merely through a count of diagnoses (p1440).
**C. Continue screening despite a prognosis shorter than the expected progression time of a polyp.** Wrong, the chapter explicitly considers discontinuation when life expectancy is shorter than the progression interval (p1440).
**D. Compare individualized life expectancy with the time needed for polyp progression to cancer.** Correct, this compares the patient's prognosis with the time horizon relevant to prevention of future cancer (p1440).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th ed., p1440.

q: What minimum lymph-node count defines adequate evaluation in the cited CRC surgical analysis?
o: A lower node-count standard solely because of age
No minimum node count for older adults
Examination of no lymph nodes after hemicolectomy
Examination of at least 12 lymph nodes
explanation:
The cited SEER analysis defines adequate lymph-node evaluation as examination of at least 12 lymph nodes (p1440).

B. No minimum node count for older adults: The analysis uses at least 12 nodes and links inadequate evaluation with inferior survival (p1440).
C. Examination of no lymph nodes after hemicolectomy: At least 12 nodes are required for adequate evaluation in the cited analysis (p1440).
A. A lower node-count standard solely because of age: Older adults were less likely to receive adequate evaluation, not assigned a lower adequacy standard (p1440).

q: Is oxaliplatin's adjuvant survival benefit established equally in all older adults?
o: Yes - the MOSAIC older subgroup gained survival from adding oxaliplatin
No - several older-subgroup analyses show no added survival benefit
Yes - the updated ACCENT analysis established survival benefit in older subgroups
No - the chapter reserves oxaliplatin for adults with substantial comorbidity
explanation:
Older-subgroup evidence on adjuvant oxaliplatin is mixed; several analyses show no added survival benefit, and it can be considered for fit adults with minimal comorbidity (p1441).

A. Yes - the MOSAIC older subgroup gained survival from adding oxaliplatin: ACCENT, MOSAIC older-subgroup and NSABP C-07 findings do not establish this uniform benefit (p1441).
D. No - the chapter reserves oxaliplatin for adults with substantial comorbidity: The text allows consideration for fit adults with minimal comorbidities (p1441).
C. Yes - the updated ACCENT analysis established survival benefit in older subgroups: The updated ACCENT analysis showed no DFS or OS benefit among older adults (p1441).

q: Which oxaliplatin toxicity can undermine function and increase falls?
o: Peripheral neuropathy
Biliary obstruction
Liver enzyme elevations
Hemolytic uremic syndrome
explanation:
**Oxaliplatin-induced peripheral neuropathy** can turn treatment toxicity into a functional problem. Hazzard says this neuropathy “may increase the risk of falls and limit functional status”; the consequence matters because falls and impaired function are themselves associated with poorer prognosis in older adults with colon cancer (p. 1441).

**A. Peripheral neuropathy.** Correct, it is the treatment-related neurologic toxicity directly linked to falls and functional limitation in this population (p. 1441).
**B. Biliary obstruction.** Wrong, it does not identify the oxaliplatin neurotoxicity linked to falls; the chapter discusses biliary obstruction as a different clinical problem requiring palliation (pp. 1441, 1446).
**C. Liver enzyme elevations.** Wrong, it substitutes a hepatic laboratory toxicity for the peripheral-nerve toxicity that explains the functional outcome in the stem (pp. 1441, 1445).
**D. Hemolytic uremic syndrome.** Wrong, it substitutes a different drug-associated syndrome for the oxaliplatin neuropathy explicitly linked to falls and functional impairment (pp. 1441, 1445).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th ed., pp. 1441, 1445, 1446.

q: What pancreatic-cancer diagnostic shortcut can incorrectly assign a poor prognosis?
o: Offering genetic testing regardless of age or family history
Omitting accurate tissue confirmation to spare diagnostic discomfort
Obtaining tissue confirmation before assigning a prognosis
Considering surgical resection in carefully selected older adults
explanation:
Omitting accurate pathologic confirmation can lead to misdiagnosis of pancreatic cancer and an incorrect poor prognosis in older adults (p1445).

C. Obtaining tissue confirmation before assigning a prognosis: The text warns about foregoing accurate pathologic diagnosis, not obtaining it (p1445).
A. Offering genetic testing regardless of age or family history: This is a described practice based on inherited susceptibility data, not the diagnostic shortcut (p1445).
D. Considering surgical resection in carefully selected older adults: The text supports potentially curative surgery in selected adults; the shortcut is lack of tissue confirmation (p1445).

q: What is the potentially curative treatment for localized pancreatic cancer?
o: Celiac plexus neurolysis
Surgical resection
Biliary stenting
Microencapsulated lipase
explanation:
Surgical resection is the only potentially curative therapy for localized pancreatic cancer and can be safe in carefully selected older adults (p1445).

C. Biliary stenting: Stenting relieves biliary obstruction as palliative care (p1446).
D. Microencapsulated lipase: Lipase supplements address pancreatic insufficiency symptoms (p1446).
A. Celiac plexus neurolysis: Neurolysis is described for pain management (p1446).

q: Which rare serious toxicity is described for gemcitabine?
o: Febrile neutropenia
Hemolytic uremic syndrome
Sensory neuropathy
Gastric outlet obstruction
explanation:
Gemcitabine can cause liver enzyme elevations and rarely hemolytic uremic syndrome (p1445).

C. Sensory neuropathy: This is listed among FOLFIRINOX side effects, rather than the rare gemcitabine toxicity requested (p1445).
A. Febrile neutropenia: This is listed for FOLFIRINOX; the rare gemcitabine toxicity specified is HUS (p1445).
D. Gastric outlet obstruction: This is a pancreatic-cancer palliative problem, not the rare gemcitabine toxicity (p1446).

q: Did POLO's progression-free benefit establish an overall-survival benefit in its interim analysis?
o: Yes - interim overall survival was significantly longer with olaparib
Yes - longer progression-free survival established an overall-survival benefit
No - interim overall survival did not differ between groups
No - progression-free survival was shorter with olaparib
explanation:
POLO prolonged progression-free survival, but its interim overall-survival analysis showed no difference between olaparib and placebo (p1446).

A. Yes - interim overall survival was significantly longer with olaparib: The interim OS comparison showed no difference (p1446).
D. No - progression-free survival was shorter with olaparib: PFS was significantly longer with olaparib (p1446).
B. Yes - longer progression-free survival established an overall-survival benefit: The book reports the two endpoints separately and no interim OS difference (p1446).

q: Does the chapter describe age as an absolute exclusion from esophageal surgery?
o: Yes - most studies make age an absolute exclusion from surgery
No - the studies generally show age to be protective against postoperative mortality
Yes - most studies exclude older adults regardless of overall fitness
No - most, but not all, studies suggest age is not a limiting factor
explanation:
Esophagectomy requires assessment of functional reserve, comorbidities and operative risk. **Most studies did not identify chronological age alone as an absolute exclusion**, although results were not uniform.

**A. Age is an absolute exclusion.** Many selected older adults underwent surgery with acceptable outcomes.
**B. Age protects against mortality.** Absence of an age cutoff does not make advanced age protective.
**C. Exclude regardless of fitness.** Fitness and performance status materially affect the comparison.
**D. Age usually is not the limiting factor.** Individual assessment accommodates studies with differing morbidity and mortality findings.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1449.

q: What core process causes MDS-associated cytopenias?
o: Ineffective clonal hematopoiesis with impaired maturation and differentiation
Destruction of red cells by CLL-associated autoantibodies
A stable diabetic nephropathy satisfying myeloma end-organ criteria
Effective hematopoiesis with unrestricted maturation of affected lineages
explanation:
MDS consists of clonal disorders with ineffective hematopoiesis and impaired maturation and differentiation, producing cytopenias (p1483).

D. Effective hematopoiesis with unrestricted maturation of affected lineages: Affected MDS lineages cannot undergo normal maturation and differentiation (p1483).
B. Destruction of red cells by CLL-associated autoantibodies: This is a CLL autoimmune mechanism, not the defining MDS process (p1492).
C. A stable diabetic nephropathy satisfying myeloma end-organ criteria: Stable diabetic nephropathy is a competing explanation, not myeloma-related damage or the MDS mechanism (p1503).
chapterTitle: Hematologic Malignancies (Leukemia/Lymphoma) and Plasma Cell Disorders

q: What confirms suspected MDS?
o: Risk scoring without obtaining a diagnostic marrow sample
Peripheral blood smear alone without marrow examination
Bone marrow biopsy with cytogenetic analysis
Serum vitamin B12 testing alone without marrow examination
explanation:
Confirmation of **myelodysplastic syndrome** requires bone marrow biopsy with cytogenetic analysis. Peripheral cytopenias or dysplastic cells raise suspicion, but marrow examination evaluates dysplasia and cytogenetic abnormalities that are central to diagnosis and disease characterization; blood tests also help exclude alternative causes of cytopenia (p1484).
"A bone marrow biopsy with cytogenetic analysis is required to confirm the diagnosis." (p1484).

**A. Risk scoring without obtaining a diagnostic marrow sample.** Wrong, risk scoring uses marrow and cytogenetic findings after diagnostic assessment; it cannot supply those missing findings on its own (p1484).
**B. Peripheral blood smear alone without marrow examination.** Wrong, a smear can suggest dysplasia but cannot replace the required marrow and cytogenetic assessment for confirmation (p1484).
**C. Bone marrow biopsy with cytogenetic analysis.** Correct, this provides the marrow morphology and chromosome information required to confirm the suspected disorder (p1484).
**D. Serum vitamin B12 testing alone without marrow examination.** Wrong, B12 testing assesses a potential megaloblastic mimic; it neither demonstrates marrow dysplasia nor supplies the required cytogenetic findings (p1484).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th ed., p1484.
chapterTitle: Hematologic Malignancies (Leukemia/Lymphoma) and Plasma Cell Disorders

q: Does early worsening of counts necessarily mean hypomethylating therapy has failed?
o: Yes - eventual responders often show improved counts during their first treatment cycle
No - hypomethylating therapy often improves counts without an initial phase of myelosuppression
No - myelosuppression often worsens for several months before a response becomes detectable
Yes - treatment-related myelosuppression often indicates that a later response will not occur
explanation:
Hypomethylating therapy can initially suppress marrow function in MDS. **Cytopenias may worsen for several months before a response becomes apparent**, so early worsening alone need not mean failure.

**A. Responders improve in cycle one.** A delayed response is possible even when counts initially worsen.
**B. No initial myelosuppression.** Early treatment can further depress already low counts.
**C. Delayed response after worsening.** Monitor counts and complications while assessing response across cycles.
**D. Myelosuppression excludes later response.** Treatment-related cytopenias can precede benefit and are not conclusive evidence of resistance.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1485.
chapterTitle: Hematologic Malignancies (Leukemia/Lymphoma) and Plasma Cell Disorders

q: Does older age alone mean AML therapy offers no survival benefit?
o: No - chemotherapy offers a potential survival benefit over supportive care for many older adults
Yes - clinical-trial evidence generally favors supportive care over chemotherapy for survival in older adults
No - older and younger adults generally experience similar treatment-related morbidity and mortality with chemotherapy
Yes - population-based evidence generally favors supportive care rather than chemotherapy for survival in older adults
explanation:
AML therapy can be beneficial in selected older adults even though toxicity is more common. **Chemotherapy can offer a survival advantage over supportive care** when disease and patient factors favor treatment.

**A. Potential survival benefit.** Treatment suitability depends on reserve, comorbidities, cognition, disease biology and goals.
**B. Trials generally favor support alone.** Evidence supports a benefit from active therapy in selected patients rather than a blanket preference for supportive care.
**C. Same treatment risk across ages.** Older adults have higher average treatment-related morbidity and mortality.
**D. Population studies favor support alone.** Observational comparisons also support treatment benefit in selected older adults, while selection affects interpretation.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1487.
chapterTitle: Hematologic Malignancies (Leukemia/Lymphoma) and Plasma Cell Disorders

q: Is a bone marrow biopsy usually required to diagnose CLL?
o: Yes - peripheral blood immunophenotyping is generally insufficient for establishing the diagnosis
No - the clinical history is generally sufficient without obtaining blood immunophenotyping
No - peripheral blood evaluation and flow cytometry generally suffice for diagnosis
Yes - bone marrow evaluation is generally a prerequisite for establishing CLL
explanation:
CLL is usually diagnosed from persistent clonal B-cell lymphocytosis in peripheral blood. **CBC, smear and blood flow cytometry generally suffice**, without routine marrow biopsy.

**A. Blood immunophenotyping insufficient.** Flow cytometry can establish the characteristic clonal B-cell phenotype.
**B. Clinical history alone.** Symptoms and examination cannot demonstrate clonality or immunophenotype.
**C. Blood evaluation and flow cytometry.** Combine the circulating cell count, morphology and phenotype with the clinical context.
**D. Marrow always required.** Marrow evaluation can clarify selected cytopenias but is not a routine diagnostic prerequisite.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1490.
chapterTitle: Hematologic Malignancies (Leukemia/Lymphoma) and Plasma Cell Disorders

q: Does isolated CLL leukocytosis mandate treatment?
o: Yes - mature circulating CLL lymphocytes generally produce leukostasis that warrants treatment
No - isolated leukocytosis without other treatment indications does not require therapy
No - symptomatic CLL progression is generally managed without disease-directed therapeutic intervention
Yes - the absolute lymphocyte count outweighs its rate of increase in treatment decisions
explanation:
Isolated CLL lymphocytosis can be observed when there is no symptomatic or progressive disease. **A high count alone does not mandate treatment**.

**A. Mature cells cause leukostasis.** Leukostasis is uncommon with the small, mature lymphocytes of CLL.
**B. Observe isolated leukocytosis.** Monitor trends, symptoms, adenopathy and cytopenias to identify evolving treatment indications.
**C. Observe symptomatic progression routinely.** Disease-related symptoms or progressive cytopenias can warrant treatment.
**D. Absolute count overrides growth rate.** Rapid change can provide more information about disease activity than a single count.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1491.
chapterTitle: Hematologic Malignancies (Leukemia/Lymphoma) and Plasma Cell Disorders

q: Why is fine-needle aspiration insufficient for lymphoma subtyping?
o: PET imaging replaces morphologic and immunophenotypic tissue assessment
Fine-needle aspiration is generally unhelpful even for an initial reactive-versus-malignant distinction
CBC findings generally provide the tissue classification needed for lymphoma subtyping
Subtyping requires adequate tissue for complex pathologic studies
explanation:
Lymphoma classification depends on architecture, cytology, immunophenotype and sometimes genetic studies. **Obtain adequate tissue for subtype determination**, often through an excisional or sufficiently large core biopsy.

**A. PET replaces pathology.** Imaging can select a biopsy site but cannot provide architecture or immunophenotype.
**B. Fine-needle aspiration is never informative.** Cytology can suggest reactive versus malignant disease while still being inadequate for full classification.
**C. CBC provides tissue subtype.** Peripheral counts do not show lymph-node architecture.
**D. Adequate tissue for complex studies.** Sufficient material permits the integrated pathologic assessment that determines subtype and treatment.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1494.
chapterTitle: Hematologic Malignancies (Leukemia/Lymphoma) and Plasma Cell Disorders

q: Why does diabetic nephropathy not automatically establish myeloma-related renal damage?
o: Diabetic nephropathy generally removes renal function from the myeloma assessment
Renal impairment is counted as myeloma end-organ damage without establishing its cause
A monoclonal protein generally attributes coexisting diabetic renal damage to myeloma
The renal damage must be attributable to the plasma-cell disorder
explanation:
**Attribution of organ damage** matters when a monoclonal protein is detected. Renal impairment counts toward myeloma-related organ damage only when it is related to the plasma-cell disorder; established diabetic nephropathy with stable renal function can explain the impairment instead. Renal function must still be assessed, because finding a monoclonal protein calls for evaluation of organ damage (p. 1503).
"The identification of a monoclonal protein requires evaluation for the presence of end-organ damage." (p. 1503).

**A. Diabetic nephropathy generally removes renal function from the myeloma assessment.** Wrong, diabetic nephropathy supplies an alternative cause, but it does not remove the need to assess renal function during evaluation of a monoclonal protein (p. 1503).
**B. Renal impairment is counted as myeloma end-organ damage without establishing its cause.** Wrong, renal impairment from an established alternative cause does not satisfy the myeloma-related organ-damage criterion merely because it is present (p. 1503).
**C. A monoclonal protein generally attributes coexisting diabetic renal damage to myeloma.** Wrong, a monoclonal protein triggers evaluation; it does not prove that coexisting renal impairment is caused by the plasma-cell disorder (p. 1503).
**D. The renal damage must be attributable to the plasma-cell disorder.** Correct, this preserves the required causal attribution and avoids labeling established, stable diabetic nephropathy as myeloma damage (p. 1503).

Source: Hazzard's Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8e (marked), pp. 1503.
chapterTitle: Hematologic Malignancies (Leukemia/Lymphoma) and Plasma Cell Disorders

q: What is the most common cause of Cushing syndrome in older patients?
o: Rapid withdrawal of chronic glucocorticoids
A benign pituitary macroadenoma causing hormone deficiency
Iatrogenic supraphysiologic corticosteroid dosing
Autoimmune adrenalitis
explanation:
**Cushing syndrome reflects glucocorticoid excess**, including exposure to supraphysiologic corticosteroid doses (p. 1530). Older patients are particularly susceptible because glucocorticoid metabolism is decreased and frailty, sarcopenia, and osteopenia are common; “The most common cause of Cushing syndrome is iatrogenic.” (p. 1530).

**A. Rapid withdrawal of chronic glucocorticoids.** Wrong, withdrawal after chronic steroid suppression concerns inadequate glucocorticoid availability, not the excess exposure defining Cushing syndrome (pp. 1530–1531).
**B. A benign pituitary macroadenoma causing hormone deficiency.** Wrong, the specified hormone-deficient macroadenoma produces hypopituitarism; that deficiency pattern does not explain glucocorticoid excess (pp. 1529–1530).
**C. Iatrogenic supraphysiologic corticosteroid dosing.** Correct, supraphysiologic prescribed corticosteroids create the excess exposure defining the syndrome and are identified as its most common cause (p. 1530).
**D. Autoimmune adrenalitis.** Wrong, autoimmune adrenalitis is a cause of primary adrenal insufficiency, which is glucocorticoid deficiency rather than Cushing syndrome (pp. 1530–1531).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8e, pp. 1529, 1530, 1531.
chapterTitle: Aging of the Endocrine System and Non-Thyroid Endocrine Disorders

q: What is the most common cause of adrenal insufficiency in older patients?
o: Autoimmune adrenalitis
Tuberculosis affecting the adrenal glands
Bilateral adrenal hemorrhage
Rapid discontinuation of chronic glucocorticoid therapy
explanation:
Rapid discontinuation of chronic glucocorticoid treatment is the most common cause of adrenal insufficiency in older patients (p1526, p1531).

A. Autoimmune adrenalitis: Although a common cause of primary adrenal insufficiency in industrialized countries, it rarely occurs in older patients (p1531).
B. Tuberculosis affecting the adrenal glands: This remains common worldwide but is very rare in older residents of industrialized countries (p1531).
C. Bilateral adrenal hemorrhage: This can occur in older anticoagulated patients, but iatrogenic suppression and withdrawal are the most common cause (p1531).
chapterTitle: Aging of the Endocrine System and Non-Thyroid Endocrine Disorders

q: An older patient has a newly identified pituitary macroincidentaloma at least 1 cm in size. Which evaluation follows Hazzard’s recommendation for a lesion of this size?
o: Assess symptoms of hormone excess and serum prolactin, leaving the other pituitary hormone axes unassessed.
Assess pituitary hormone deficiency for a solid lesion, but omit that assessment if the lesion is cystic.
Arrange serial sellar imaging for anatomical follow-up, deferring the initial pituitary hormone deficiency assessment.
Assess hormone excess and prolactin, adding a careful evaluation for pituitary hormone deficiencies.
explanation:
A pituitary macroincidentaloma can secrete hormones or compress normal pituitary tissue. **Evaluate for hormone excess and prolactin elevation, and assess pituitary hormone deficiencies** in a lesion at least 1 cm.

**A. Excess and prolactin alone.** This may identify hypersecretion but misses compression-related hypopituitarism.
**B. Test deficiency only if solid.** A cystic macroincidentaloma can also impair pituitary function.
**C. Imaging without hormonal assessment.** Serial imaging measures anatomy, not hormone reserve.
**D. Assess excess and deficiencies.** Evaluate both secretory behavior and deficits that may need replacement.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1529.
chapterTitle: Aging of the Endocrine System and Non-Thyroid Endocrine Disorders

q: What CT finding on an adrenal incidentaloma excludes malignancy and pheochromocytoma?
o: Any radiodensity in an incidentally discovered mass
An adrenal mass larger than 4 cm
Low radiodensity, below 10 Hounsfield units
Higher radiodensity requiring biochemical evaluation
explanation:
Low adrenal-incidentaloma radiodensity from fat content, below 10 Hounsfield units on CT, excludes malignancy and pheochromocytoma in the book (p1532).

D. Higher radiodensity requiring biochemical evaluation: Higher-density incidentalomas must be assessed for pheochromocytoma (p1532).
B. An adrenal mass larger than 4 cm: Masses larger than 4 cm are more likely to be malignant (p1532).
A. Any radiodensity in an incidentally discovered mass: All incidentalomas require assessment; the exclusion described is low radiodensity below 10 units (p1532).
chapterTitle: Aging of the Endocrine System and Non-Thyroid Endocrine Disorders

q: Why is hematocrit monitored during testosterone treatment in an older man?
o: To detect treatment-induced erythrocytosis and guide dose reduction or interruption
To confirm cognitive improvement and guide escalation when memory is unchanged
To establish long-term cardiovascular safety and guide continuation without reassessment
To select a formulation that can be continued despite an adverse effect
explanation:
Testosterone increases erythropoiesis, sometimes excessively. **Monitor hematocrit to detect erythrocytosis and guide dose reduction or interruption** before continued exposure worsens it.

**A. Detect erythrocytosis.** A rising hematocrit is an actionable safety finding, particularly beyond 54%.
**B. Measure cognition.** Hematocrit does not measure cognitive response and unchanged memory is no reason to escalate the dose.
**C. Prove cardiovascular safety.** A normal hematocrit alone cannot exclude all cardiovascular risk.
**D. Continue any formulation despite toxicity.** An adverse effect may require interruption, which can be harder with long-acting preparations.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1535–1536.
chapterTitle: Aging of the Endocrine System and Non-Thyroid Endocrine Disorders

q: Is PSA/DRE monitoring recommended for a 74-year-old man starting testosterone therapy?
o: Yes - age 70 or older is the usual indication for routine PSA/DRE screening during therapy
No - such screening is not recommended at age 70 or older
No - starting testosterone generally removes screening from consideration even before age 70
Yes - short life expectancy strengthens the routine screening indication
explanation:
Population screening, pretreatment assessment and follow-up of an abnormal result are different decisions. **Do not institute automatic serial PSA and DRE screening solely because this 74-year-old starts testosterone.** Still evaluate prostate history, symptoms, baseline risk and applicable pretreatment guidance.

**A. Age over 70 is an indication for routine screening.** Age alone does not create a serial screening indication. Consider life expectancy, risk and preferences.
**B. No routine screening after 70.** A routine series of screening tests is a different decision from baseline safety assessment. A pretreatment PSA is recommended for men over 40, and later PSA testing depends on individual risk and preferences.
**C. Testosterone eliminates screening in younger men.** It does not remove the need to consider risk-appropriate baseline assessment or screening.
**D. Short life expectancy strengthens screening.** Less time to benefit generally reduces the value of screening, while downstream harms remain immediate.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1536. AUA Testosterone Deficiency Guideline, statements 12 and 30, and follow-up testing guidance.
chapterTitle: Aging of the Endocrine System and Non-Thyroid Endocrine Disorders

q: An older outpatient has primary hyperparathyroidism caused by a single parathyroid adenoma. Which process explains this disorder?
o: Compensatory PTH secretion in response to low serum calcium
Autonomous PTH secretion from abnormal parathyroid tissue
Parathyroid hyperplasia after longstanding severe secondary hyperparathyroidism
Specimen acidosis during delayed processing of an ionized-calcium sample
explanation:
**Primary hyperparathyroidism** arises from autonomous secretion of PTH by abnormal parathyroid tissue, producing hypercalcemia. This differs from a compensatory response to low calcium and from autonomy that develops after longstanding secondary hyperparathyroidism (p. 1536). The deciding distinction is "autonomous pathologic hypersecretion of PTH and hypercalcemia" (p. 1536).

**A. Compensatory PTH secretion in response to low serum calcium.** Wrong, this describes secondary hyperparathyroidism, a physiologic response to hypocalcemia; it does not explain autonomous secretion by the adenoma (p. 1536).
**B. Autonomous PTH secretion from abnormal parathyroid tissue.** Correct, the adenoma is the abnormal parathyroid tissue driving autonomous hormone secretion and hypercalcemia in this patient (p. 1536).
**C. Parathyroid hyperplasia after longstanding severe secondary hyperparathyroidism.** Wrong, this describes tertiary hyperparathyroidism after severe chronic secondary disease, rather than primary disease caused by an adenoma (p. 1536).
**D. Specimen acidosis during delayed processing of an ionized-calcium sample.** Wrong, this can falsely elevate measured ionized calcium through poor specimen handling; it is a measurement artifact rather than the mechanism of the diagnosed adenoma (p. 1536).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th ed., p. 1536.
chapterTitle: Aging of the Endocrine System and Non-Thyroid Endocrine Disorders

q: What serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D level defines vitamin D sufficiency per the American Geriatrics Society (used for fall/fracture prevention in frail older adults)?
o: Less than 12 ng/mL
Greater than 20 ng/mL
12 to 20 ng/mL
Greater than 30 ng/mL
explanation:
The AGS definition used for fall and fracture prevention in frail high-risk older adults is serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D greater than 30 ng/mL (p1539).

B. Greater than 20 ng/mL: This is the Institute of Medicine sufficiency definition for general-population bone health (p1539).
C. 12 to 20 ng/mL: The Institute of Medicine defines this as insufficiency (p1539).
A. Less than 12 ng/mL: The Institute of Medicine defines this as deficiency (p1539).
chapterTitle: Aging of the Endocrine System and Non-Thyroid Endocrine Disorders

q: Does TSH rising with normal aging indicate occult thyroid failure?
o: Yes - normal aging generally lowers free T4 as TSH rises
Yes - rising TSH with stable free T4 proves occult failure
No - TSH generally decreases in euthyroid aging without underlying thyroid disease
No - free T4 remains unchanged in euthyroid aging
explanation:
A modest age-related rise in **TSH** does not itself demonstrate occult thyroid failure in otherwise euthyroid people. The key observation is that free T4 remains stable. The chapter suggests altered TSH bioactivity or thyroidal sensitivity as possible explanations, rather than a fall in circulating free T4 (p1546).
"The increase in TSH with normal aging does not indicate occult thyroid failure, since free T4 levels do not decline." (p1546).
"Instead, there may be changes in the bioactivity of TSH or thyroidal sensitivity to TSH." (p1546).

**A. Yes - normal aging generally lowers free T4 as TSH rises.** Wrong, the stated normal-aging pattern preserves free T4; a falling free T4 is not the pattern described in this question (p1546).
**B. Yes - rising TSH with stable free T4 proves occult failure.** Wrong, stable free T4 accompanying an age-related TSH increase does not prove occult failure; the chapter explicitly rejects that interpretation (p1546).
**C. No - TSH generally decreases in euthyroid aging without underlying thyroid disease.** Wrong, TSH gradually increases, not decreases, in the euthyroid population described (p1546).
**D. No - free T4 remains unchanged in euthyroid aging.** Correct, unchanged free T4 is the reason the chapter gives for not interpreting the normal-aging TSH rise as occult thyroid failure (p1546).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th ed., p1546.

q: A patient on 112 μg levothyroxine daily has a rising TSH. Before assuming disease progression, what simple explanation should be checked?
o: An unchanged average dose despite missing a weekly tablet
Absence of a TSH response to missed replacement doses
Missed doses and difficulty with adherence
Increased exposure from missing a weekly tablet
explanation:
Adherence should be considered first when TSH varies; missing one weekly dose of 112 micrograms reduces the daily average to 96 micrograms (p1552).

A. An unchanged average dose despite missing a weekly tablet: The prescribed 112-microgram dose does not ensure the delivered average if doses are missed (p1552).
D. Increased exposure from missing a weekly tablet: The example lowers the average from 112 to 96 micrograms (p1552).
B. Absence of a TSH response to missed replacement doses: The text discusses TSH elevation after stabilization and checking adherence and interacting conditions (p1552).

q: In managing myxedema coma, what is the critical sequencing error to avoid regarding hydrocortisone and thyroid hormone?
o: Initiating hydrocortisone to cover potentially impaired adrenal reserve
Giving thyroid hormone without hydrocortisone when adrenal reserve is impaired
Obtaining serum for cortisol measurement before starting hydrocortisone
Stopping hydrocortisone after the cortisol level is found adequate
explanation:
Thyroid hormone without hydrocortisone can precipitate adrenal crisis when adrenal reserve is impaired in myxedema coma (p1553).

C. Obtaining serum for cortisol measurement before starting hydrocortisone: The book recommends obtaining serum and then initiating IV hydrocortisone (p1553).
A. Initiating hydrocortisone to cover potentially impaired adrenal reserve: This is the recommended protection against adrenal crisis (p1553).
D. Stopping hydrocortisone after the cortisol level is found adequate: The book permits stopping it once cortisol is found adequate (p1553).

q: Before using the rheumatoid-arthritis classification score in Hazzard Table 101-1, which clinical entry conditions must be met?
o: Joint pain may replace clinical synovitis when rheumatoid factor is positive
Clinical synovitis qualifies even when another disease explains it better
Positive anti-CCP antibodies qualify even without any clinical joint synovitis
Definite clinical synovitis must be present without a better alternative explanation
explanation:
**Rheumatoid-arthritis classification** starts with clinical entry conditions before interpreting the score. The table requires "at least 1 joint with definite clinical synovitis" and "the synovitis not better explained by another disease". This prevents a score or antibody result from substituting for the required clinical setting; the accompanying text notes that anti-CCP antibodies can occur in healthy people before clinical RA (last application is an inference, p. 1608).

**A. Joint pain may replace clinical synovitis when rheumatoid factor is positive.** Wrong, the table requires definite clinical synovitis; pain and positive rheumatoid factor do not replace that entry condition (p. 1608).
**B. Clinical synovitis qualifies even when another disease explains it better.** Wrong, the table explicitly excludes synovitis better explained by another disease, so this option drops an essential condition (p. 1608).
**C. Positive anti-CCP antibodies qualify even without any clinical joint synovitis.** Wrong, clinical synovitis is still required, and the text notes that these antibodies can be present in healthy individuals before clinical RA (p. 1608).
**D. Definite clinical synovitis must be present without a better alternative explanation.** Correct, this retains both entry conditions before the classification score is applied (p. 1608).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th ed., p. 1608.

q: How useful is anti-CCP antibody testing for distinguishing LORA from polymyalgia rheumatica?
o: One small study found the same positivity in LORA, PMR and healthy older controls
One small study found positivity in 65% of PMR but none of LORA or healthy controls
One small study found positivity in every LORA patient and none of the PMR patients
One small study found positivity in 65% of LORA but none of PMR or healthy controls
explanation:
In one small study, anti-CCP was positive in 65% of LORA patients but none of the PMR patients or healthy older controls, suggesting usefulness as a discriminator (p1611).

B. One small study found positivity in 65% of PMR but none of LORA or healthy controls: The 65% result belongs to LORA, not PMR (p1611).
C. One small study found positivity in every LORA patient and none of the PMR patients: The LORA result was 65%, not universal positivity (p1611).
A. One small study found the same positivity in LORA, PMR and healthy older controls: The groups differed: 65% in LORA and none in the other two groups (p1611).

A. Protection of the cervical spine by long-standing RA: The book describes increased risk of cervical disease and instability (p1612).

q: Which interpretation best explains the association between Sjögren syndrome and lymphoma described in Hazzard?
o: Chronic T-cell stimulation drives the predominantly T-cell malignant transformation.
Loss of autoantibodies signals restoration of the normal antibody-producing population.
A monoclonal IgM spike reflects resolution of the benign exocrine process.
Chronic B-cell stimulation drives progression from benign exocrinopathy toward lymphoma.
explanation:
Sjögren syndrome causes autoimmune inflammation of exocrine glands, particularly the salivary and lacrimal glands. **Persistent B-cell stimulation** is a proposed explanation for how a reactive glandular infiltrate can give rise to a malignant B-cell clone.

**A. T-cell transformation.** T cells participate in glandular inflammation, but the lymphomas associated with Sjögren syndrome arise predominantly from B cells.
**B. Loss of autoantibodies.** Autoantibody levels can fall when lymphoma cells displace normal antibody-producing plasma cells. Falling levels can therefore accompany progression.
**C. Monoclonal IgM signals recovery.** A new monoclonal IgM band indicates production by one clone and may herald lymphoma. It warrants evaluation.
**D. Chronic B-cell stimulation.** Persistent glandular lymphoid proliferation can pass through a reactive stage called pseudolymphoma before a malignant clone emerges.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1626.

q: An older adult with osteoporosis develops height loss and kyphosis without recalling severe back pain. Which interpretation is best supported?
o: The absence of severe pain makes a slowly developing vertebral fracture an unlikely explanation.
The height loss and kyphosis support suspicion of a slowly developing vertebral fracture.
The absence of neurological signs makes an osteoporotic vertebral fracture an unlikely explanation.
The absence of a recalled fall makes an osteoporotic vertebral fracture an unlikely explanation.
explanation:
Osteoporotic vertebral bodies can collapse gradually with little or no pain. **New height loss and increasing kyphosis warrant evaluation for vertebral fracture**, even when the patient cannot recall an acute painful episode.

**A. No severe pain.** Abrupt collapse can cause intense pain, whereas gradual compression may first come to attention through a change in posture.
**B. Height loss and kyphosis.** Compression reduces vertebral body height. Anterior wedging can also increase forward curvature of the thoracic spine.
**C. No neurologic signs.** Most osteoporotic compression fractures spare the neural structures, so limb strength and sensation are usually preserved.
**D. No remembered fall.** Fragile vertebrae can fracture during ordinary activity without a distinct traumatic event.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1631.

q: An older adult with an osteoporotic vertebral compression fracture has persistent severe back pain beyond the expected healing period. Which interpretation follows Hazzard?
o: Consider an additional fracture or an alternative diagnosis
Treat prolonged severe pain as evidence that healing is proceeding normally
Use the prior fracture to discount the possibility of further fractures
Require new neurologic deficits before considering another vertebral fracture
explanation:
Pain from an osteoporotic compression fracture usually eases over several weeks. When severe pain persists beyond the expected healing period, **reassess for another fracture or a different diagnosis**.

**A. Reconsider the diagnosis.** Localize the pain again. A newly painful level may indicate another fracture, and persistent focal pain can also occur with infection or malignancy.
**B. Assume normal healing.** Residual soreness can accompany recovery, but persistently severe pain lacks the expected trend toward improvement.
**C. Discount further fractures.** A previous vertebral fragility fracture increases the risk of subsequent vertebral and nonvertebral fractures.
**D. Wait for neurologic deficits.** Another compression fracture can produce severe axial pain while strength and sensation remain intact.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1631.

q: In older adults, what is a key pitfall in recognizing infectious back pain (eg, discitis/osteomyelitis)?
o: Endovascular infection risk generally favors a mechanical explanation for the presenting back pain
Disc infection generally differs sufficiently from mechanical disease to permit straightforward clinical recognition
Fever is sometimes absent despite the presence of spinal infection in older adults
Fever is generally required before spinal infection should enter the differential for back pain
explanation:
Discitis and vertebral osteomyelitis can present with back pain that resembles mechanical disease. In an older adult, **spinal infection can be present despite a normal temperature**.

**A. Endovascular risk favors mechanical pain.** Bacteremia from endocarditis or an infected vascular catheter can seed a vertebra, increasing concern for an infectious cause.
**B. Disc infection is easy to distinguish.** An infected disc can hurt with movement, just as a degenerative disc can. The pain pattern alone is a poor discriminator.
**C. Fever can be absent.** Older adults may mount only a small temperature rise despite infection of the disc or adjacent bone.
**D. Wait for fever.** New, persistent focal back pain in a patient with bacteremia warrants evaluation even if the patient remains afebrile.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1631.

q: How do you distinguish neurogenic claudication from vascular claudication on exercise testing?
o: Both conditions resolve on the treadmill because spinal extension increases canal diameter
Both conditions improve on the bicycle because spinal flexion reduces vascular symptoms
Neurogenic symptoms improve on the bicycle; vascular symptoms persist on both tests
Neurogenic symptoms persist on both tests; vascular symptoms improve on the bicycle
explanation:
Neurogenic claudication is exertional leg discomfort from lumbar spinal stenosis that varies with spinal posture. **Cycling in a flexed position often relieves neurogenic symptoms. Vascular claudication can occur on both tests** when the leg workload is sufficient.

**A. Both improve on the treadmill.** Lumbar extension narrows the canal, so upright walking can provoke neurogenic leg symptoms.
**B. Both improve on the bicycle.** Leaning forward widens the spinal canal but cannot correct limited arterial blood flow to exercising muscles.
**C. Bicycle relief favors neurogenic pain.** Improvement when the patient bends forward while continuing to pedal points to posture-dependent neural compression.
**D. Bicycle relief favors vascular pain.** Vascular symptoms improve when muscular demand falls with rest. Changing spinal posture alone offers little relief.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1636.

q: Why is lumbar spine imaging a poor stand-alone diagnostic tool in older adults?
o: A herniated nucleus pulposus generally establishes the cause of the presenting symptoms
Lumbar imaging abnormalities are common in asymptomatic older adults
A disc bulge on MRI is usually sufficient to attribute the clinical pain to that level
Disc degeneration is uncommon among asymptomatic people older than 60
explanation:
Lumbar imaging shows structural changes that become common with age, including in people who have no back pain. **Match the level and side of a lesion to the symptoms and examination** before attributing pain to it.

**A. A herniation explains the symptoms.** A herniation is more convincing when the affected root matches the distribution of radiating pain or weakness.
**B. Abnormalities in pain-free older adults.** The same MRI finding can occur with or without symptoms, limiting its specificity for the cause of pain.
**C. A bulge identifies the painful level.** Bulges may appear at multiple levels. The scan alone cannot tell which, if any, is symptomatic.
**D. Degeneration is rare in pain-free adults over 60.** One study found disc degeneration in 93 percent of asymptomatic participants older than 60.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1636.

q: In the epidural steroid injection RCT of 400 older adults with lumbar spinal stenosis, what did adding glucocorticoid to lidocaine achieve?
o: Proof that lidocaine alone has no effect compared with placebo
Minimal or no additional short-term disability or leg-pain benefit
Proof that steroid injections outperform a placebo injection
A clear additional short-term disability and leg-pain benefit
explanation:
The 400-patient trial found minimal or no additional short-term disability or leg-pain benefit from adding glucocorticoid to lidocaine; it had no placebo arm (p1639).

D. A clear additional short-term disability and leg-pain benefit: The reported comparison showed minimal or no short-term benefit (p1639).
C. Proof that steroid injections outperform a placebo injection: The trial included no placebo group (p1639).
A. Proof that lidocaine alone has no effect compared with placebo: Without a placebo arm, that comparison was not made (p1639).

At eight-year SPORT follow-up, 52% of those randomized to nonoperative treatment had undergone surgery (p1639).

A. 36%: This is herniated nucleus pulposus prevalence in an asymptomatic over-60 MRI sample (p1636).
C. 21%: This is spinal stenosis prevalence in that asymptomatic sample (p1636).
